name: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
credit: Page from the Codex Palatinus graecus 23 (the Palatine Anthology), 10th century, folio 5 recto, used here as an illustration of the Anthology itself, not a portrait · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Greek Anthology is the great collection of some four thousand short Greek poems, mostly epigrams, written between the archaic age and the Byzantine Middle Ages. Its main source is the tenth-century Palatine manuscript, itself built on earlier anthologies by Meleager, Philippus and Agathias.

This file gathers the epigrams in Books I–VI of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1916) whose author is not named, is not dated in Paton's index of authors, or is disputed. Where Paton names a possible author, the note on the poem says so.

poems.title: Book I, 1: Inscribed on the Tabernacle of Saint Sophia
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The images that the heretics took down from here our pious sovereigns replaced.

poems.title: Book I, 2: Inscribed on the Apse of Blachernae
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The divine Justin, the husband of Sophia, to whom Christ granted the gift of restoring everything, and glory in war, finding that the temple of the Virgin Mother was tottering, took the decayed part to pieces and built it up again securely.

poems.title: Book I, 3: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This lovely temple shining with beauty the earlier Justin built to the Mother of God. A later Justin during his reign endowed it with more than its former splendour.

poems.title: Book I, 4: On the Temple of St. John the Baptist (the Forerunner) in the property of Studius
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Studius built this fair house to John the great servant of Christ, and quickly gained the reward of his work by obtaining the consular fasces.

poems.title: Book I, 5: On the Church of St. Thomas the Apostle in the property of Amantius
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This house thou didst make for God, Amantius, in the middle of the sea, combating the swirling waves. Nor south nor north wind shall shake thy holy house, guarded as it is by this divine temple. May thy days be many; for thou by invading the sea hast made New Rome more glorious.

poems.title: Book I, 6: On the Church of St. Theodore in the land of Sphoracius
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Sphoracius having escaped from a fire built this temple to the Martyr.

poems.title: Book I, 7: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Sphoracius, Antolius thy nephew rejoiced in repaying during thy life thy kindness in bringing him up, and now thou art dead ever pays thee grateful honour; so that he found for thee a new honour, and laid thee in the temple thou thyself didst build.

poems.title: Book I, 8: On the Church of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul near St. Sergius in the property of Hormisdas
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Honouring the King of Kings, Christ, with his works, Justinian built this glorious temple to Peter and Paul, for by giving honour to His servants a man offereth great glory to the King Himself. Here is profit for the soul and for the eyes. Let each get what he hath need of by his prayers, and take joy in looking at the beauty and splendour of the house.

poems.title: Book I, 9: On the Church of St. Michael in Bothreptus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: An this celebrated work too is the fruit of thy toil, skilled Gerradius. For thou didst reveal to us anew the lovely temple of the captain of the angelic host.

poems.title: Book I, 10: On the Church of the Holy Martyr Polyeuctus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Eudocia the empress, eager to honour God, first built here a temple of Polyeuctus the servant of God. But she did not make it as great and beautiful as it is, not from any economy or lack of possessions— what doth a queen lack ?—but because her prophetic soul told her that she should leave a family well knowing how better to adorn it. Whence Juliana, the glory of her blessed parents, inheriting their royal blood in the fourth generation, did not defeat the hopes of the Queen, the mother of a noble race, but raised this from a small temple to its present size and beauty, increasing the glory of her many-sceptred ancestors; for all that she made, she made more magnificent than they, holding the true faith of a mind devoted to Christ. Who hath not heard of Juliana, how in her pious care she glorified even her parents by fair-fashioned works? All alone by her righteous toil she built a worthy house to immortal Polyeuctus, for she had ever studied to give blameless gifts to all athletes of the Heavenly King. Every country cries, every city, that she made her parents more glorious by better works. Where do we not find that Juliana hath raised splendid temples to the Saints? Where do we not see the signs of the pious hand of thee alone? What place hath not learnt that thy mind is full of piety? The inhabitants of the whole world sing thy works, which are eternally remembered. For the works of piety are not hidden; oblivion doth not quench the labours of beneficent virtue. Not even thyself knoweth how many houses dedicated to God thy hand hath made ; for thou alone, I ween, didst build innumerable temples all over the world, ever fearing the servants of God in Heaven. Following by her good works all the footsteps of her parents she made the fame of her race immortal, always walking in the whole path of piety. Therefore, all ye servants of the Heavenly King to whom she gave gifts or built temples, preserve her gladly with her son and his daughters, and may the immeasurable glory of the most beneficent family survive as long as the Sun drives his burning chariot. What quire is sufficient to chant the works of Juliana, who after Constantine, the adorner of his Rome, and after the holy golden light of Theodosius, and after so many royal ancestors, in a few years accomplished a work worthy of her race, yea, more than worthy? She alone did violence to Time and surpassed the wisdom of renowned Solomon by raising a habitation for God, whose glittering and elaborate beauty the ages cannot celebrate—how it rises from its deep-rooted foundations, running up from the ground and aspiring to the stars of heaven, and how from east to west it extends itself glittering with unspeakable brightness in the sunlight on both its sides! On either side of its aisle columns standing on firm columns support the rays of the golden dome, while on each side arched recesses scattered on the dome reproduce the ever-revolving light of the moon. The opposite walls in innumerable paths are clothed in marvellous metallic veins of colour, like flowery meadows which Nature made to flower in the depth of the rock, and hid their glory, keeping them for the House of God, to be the gift of Juliana, so that she might produce a divine work, following in her toil the stainless dictates of her heart. What singer of skilful works shall now hasten to the west, armed with a hundred eyes, and read aright the various devices on the walls, gazing on the circle of the shining house, one story set on another? There you may see a marvellous creation of the holy pencils above the centre of the porch, the wise Constantine, how escaping from the ido!s he quenched the impious fury of the heathen and found the light of the Trinity by cleansing his limbs in water. Such is the labour that Juliana, after a countless swarm of labours, accomplished for the souls of her parents, and for her own life, and for that of those who are and shall be.

poems.title: Book I, 11: On the Church of the Saints Cosmas and Damian in the district of Basiliscus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thy servant Sophia, O Christ, offer this gift to thy servants. Receive thine own, and to my emperor Justin give in payment therefor victory on victory over diseases and the barbarians.

poems.title: Book I, 12: On St. Euphemia of Olybrius
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I am the House of the Trinity, and three generations built me. First Eudoxia, the daughter of Theodosius, having escaped from war and the barbarians, erected and dedicated me to God in acknowledgement of her rescue from distress. Next her daughter Placidia with her most blessed husband adorned me. Thirdly, if perchance my beauty was at all deficient in splendour, munificent Juliana invested me with it in memory of her parents, and bestowed the height of glory on her mother and father and her mother’s illustrious mother by augmenting my former adornment. Thus was I made.

poems.title: Book I, 13: IIn the same Church, inside the Gallery
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I had loveliness before, but now in addition to my former beauty I have acquired greater splendour.

poems.title: Book I, 14
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thus did Juliana, after her mother and grandmother, scrape off my coat of old age, and I have new bloom.

poems.title: Book I, 15
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: There was then something more beautful than beauty, since my fabric, even formerly of world-wide celebrity, was advanced to a beauty greater than its former splendour by Juliana, so that now it rivals the stars.

poems.title: Book I, 16
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Juliana had the Martyr herself, the Patroness of the church, to inspire and help the artificers. For never would she have accomplished otherwise so vast and beautiful a work, full of heavenly splendour.

poems.title: Book I, 17
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: No longer dost thou marvel at the glory of them who are passed away: by their art they did not leave a fame so great as is the glory of wise Juliana, who by her work surpassed the skilled design of her ancestors.

poems.title: Book I, 18: On an Uncertain Object
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I am the good circle of good Agathonike ... . and she dedicated me to the immaculate Martyr Trophimus.

poems.title: Book I, 19: To the Saviour
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: O Thou Who guardest the wise womb of the everflowing fire, Who art enthroned on the revolving necessity of the Universe, Christ, vivifying Source of the divinely appointed life, first begotten Voice of God the ineffable Father, Who, after the burden of Thy Mother’s pangs and the self-accomplished birth from a marriage without bridegroom, didst arrest the heterodox rage of the Syrian race, and dissolve the falsely named rites of empty idols, and then didst ascend the seven-zoned belt of heaven seated on the unspeakable angelic wings, have mercy on me, venerated Eye of God, the Maker of all things, Keeper of life, Saviour of men, Lord of Eternity.

poems.title: Book I, 20: To the Lord Christ
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Newly revealed, Lord of the sky, born of old time, new-born Son, ever existing and pre-existing, highest and last, Christ, coeval with Thy immortal Father, in all ways like Him.

poems.title: Book I, 21: To the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Old man, born before the ages, coeval with the Father.

poems.title: Book I, 22: To the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: All-wise Word of the heavenly Father, Lord of the world, Who didst honour the race of mankind by Thy image, grant us Thy grace and Thy help that bestoweth blessings ; for the eyes of all look to Thee in hope.

poems.title: Book I, 23
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Son, co-eternal with the immortal Father, Lord of all, who rulest over all things in Heaven, in Sea, and on Earth, give to Thy servant Marinus who wrote this book the grace of eloquence and wisdom of speech.

poems.title: Book I, 24: To the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Enthroned with Thy Father and the good Spirit and like unto Them without beginning, King of all that is, was, and shall be, give Thy grace unto him who wrote this, that by Thy precepts he may walk rightly in the path of his life.

poems.title: Book I, 25: To the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Christ, Wisdom of God, Ruler and Governor of the world, Creator of old of our human stock, vouchsafe to me to run the race of life in the way of Thy commandments.

poems.title: Book I, 26: To the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Son of God, who rulest on high, eternal Light that lighteneth, give me Thy grace now and after and ever, for that is the root of all for him to whom Thou shalt grant it in such manner as is best.

poems.title: Book I, 27: To the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Almighty Son of God, Christ, without beginning and existing before all, Who dost make to gush forth fountains of salvation for all mankind, listen to the prayers of Thy Virgin Mother, and grant us Thy grace in word and deed.

poems.title: Book I, 28
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Christ, Wisdom of God, endow with the grace of eloquence and make skilled in wisdom of speech Marinus, who wrote this volume with his own hand, a medicine for folly and guide to right diction.

poems.title: Book I, 29: To the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Shed, O Christ, Thy grace on my works. Christ shall be the helper of even my works. May Christ stretch out a helping hand to my labour. Christ, send me Thy help full of blessing. Christ, Thyself give Thy grace to my work.

poems.title: Book I, 30: To the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Blessed Christ, eternal Light of men, Hope of all, give good to them who are in need of it, and keep away evil.

poems.title: Book I, 31: To the Most Holy Mother of God
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: O Quzen, holding in thy arms thy almighty Child, the Son of God, before Whom the angels tremble, and making Him merciful in mind to men, guard Him and keep therewith the whole world safe from trouble.

poems.title: Book I, 32: To the Archangel Michael
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Hence is kept the divine help for wretched men, afflicted in mind or body. For vexing trouble at once is put to flight, Michael, by thy name, thy image, or thy house.

poems.title: Book I, 33
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: On an Image of the Archangel How daring it is to picture the incorporeal! But yet the image leads us up to spiritual recollection of celestial beings.

poems.title: Book I, 37: On the Birth of Christ
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Trumpets! Lightnings! The earth trembles! but into the Virgin’s womb thou didst descend with noiseless tread.

poems.title: Book I, 38: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The manger is Heaven, yea, greater than Heaven. Heaven is the handiwork of this child.

poems.title: Book I, 39: On the Shepherds and Angels
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: One dance, one song for men and angels, for man and God are become one.

poems.title: Book I, 40: On the Birth of Christ
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The manger is Heaven, yea, greater than Heaven, for He whom it received is the King of the Heavenly ones.

poems.title: Book I, 41: On the Magi
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: No longer do the Magi bring presents to Fire and the Sun; for this Child made Sun and Fire.

poems.title: Book I, 42: On Bethlehem
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Receive Him, Bethlehem, Him who, as the good prophet foretold, would come from thee to be the Ruler of all peoples.

poems.title: Book I, 43: On Rachel
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Why mournest thou, Rachel, shedding bitter tears? Because I see my children slain I shed tears.

poems.title: Book I, 44: On the Annunciation
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Hail, Maiden, full of grace, most blessed, Bride immaculate, thou shalt have in thy womb a Son conceived without a father.

poems.title: Book I, 45: On the Visitation
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The prophet, while yet in the womb, saw and showed by leaping that thy child was God, and his Mother gave praise.

poems.title: Book I, 46: On the Presentation
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: O man, receive the child who was born before Adam, who will deliver thee from this life and bring thee to eternal life.

poems.title: Book I, 47: On the Baptism
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: From the immortal Father the most mighty Spirit came, when the Son was being baptized in the waters of Jordan.

poems.title: Book I, 49: On Lazarus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Christ said “Come here,’ and Lazarus left Hades, recovering the breath in his dry nostrils.

poems.title: Book I, 50: On the Same, in Ephesus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: He made the Soul, and likewise fashioned the body. He brings back Lazarus from the dead into the light.

poems.title: Book I, 52: On Palm Sunday
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Hail, daughter of Zion, and look on Christ the King seated on a foal and going swiftly to his Passion.

poems.title: Book I, 53: On Easter
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Christ abolished the lamb of the law, and provided an immortal sacrifice, Himself the priest and Himself the victim.

poems.title: Book I, 54: On the Crucifixion
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: O passion, cross, O blood that purgeth of the passions, cleanse my soul from all wickedness.

poems.title: Book I, 55: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: He said that the Virgin should be the Virgin’s Son, another Himself: Have mercy on us, Lord of pure virginity.

poems.title: Book I, 56: On the Resurrection
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Christ being God took away all the dead from Hell, and left Hell the destroyer alone and soulless.

poems.title: Book I, 57: On the Lamb of God
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: On the threshold of my soul is the saving blood of the Lamb. Away, Destroyer, come not near.

poems.title: Book I, 58: On Gideon's Fleece
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: One fleece has dew ; it gave dew to the bowl; the same fleece is dewless. Hide hidden things in thy mind.

poems.title: Book I, 59: On Moses and Pharaoh's Daughter
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: An Egyptian woman, a hidden child, and water near by. These things are types of the Word only to the pious.

poems.title: Book I, 60: On the Same when he stretched forth his hands to discomfit Amalek
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Why dost thou, Moses, stretch forth thy hands in the form of a cross? By this type perish both Amaleks.

poems.title: Book I, 61: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Defend thy Gentile wife by the well, Moses, because thou art the type of the infallible bridegroom.

poems.title: Book I, 62: On the Ark passing over Jordan
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The stream yielded to the golden Ark. Have mercy on us, O Christ; the Ark is a type of thy baptism here.

poems.title: Book I, 63: On Hagar
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Hagar, too, is of the Gentiles. But what is the angel, what is the fountain?® I, too, am of the Gentiles, therefore I know these things.

poems.title: Book I, 64: On the Seventy Palms and Twelve Wells
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Know that the seventy palms and twelve wells of water are types of the number of Christ’s disciples.

poems.title: Book I, 65: On Abraham
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Abraham takes his son to. be sacrificed to God. Be merciful! What sacrifice doth the mind see of which this picture is a type ?

poems.title: Book I, 66: On Melchisedech giving Wine and Bread to Abraham
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: “King Melchisedech, priest, who art thou that givest bread and wine?”’ “A type of truth.”

poems.title: Book I, 67: On Abraham receiving God
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Here hath God only the form of a man, but later He in truth attained a human nature.

poems.title: Book I, 68: On Jacob blessing Isaac
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: His hands have smell for the Spirit, and skin for the Letter. The mind that seeth God is pleasing to a father.

poems.title: Book I, 69: On Rebecca
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Only begotten bridegroom, thy Gentile bride, loving thee, leapt down from the height of an unclean body.

poems.title: Book I, 70: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The lady Rebecca was wooed not far from the water, because she is the type of a Gentile bride.

poems.title: Book I, 71: On the Shunamite
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The prayer of Elisha, O Shunamite, twice gave thee thy son, first from thy womb, and next from the dead.

poems.title: Book I, 72: On Elijah’s Mantle
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This skin foretells the Lamb of God, who shall be baptized here for the life of all men.

poems.title: Book I, 73: On David being Anointed
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I KNow in my heart, but fear to utter, whose father this David was called, whom thou seest anointed here.

poems.title: Book I, 74: On the Blind Man
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The name of the pool is Sent, but dost thou understand who is sent by whom, so that thou mayest have a perfect view ?

poems.title: Book I, 75: On the Samaritan Woman
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: No type, but a God and bridegroom here saves his Gentile bride, whom he saw beside the water.

poems.title: Book I, 76: On the Wedding
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: God truly made wine, but the mystery of the miracle thou understandest if the spirit of Christ possesses thee.

poems.title: Book I, 77: On the Widow who fed Elijah
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The cruse of oil and the barrel of meal overflow because the widow has firm faith.

poems.title: Book I, 78: On Peter the Apostle
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Peter is the high-priest of all the high-priests of God, having received this office by the voice of God.

poems.title: Book I, 79: On Paul the Apostle
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Paul, having seen face to face the divine light of Heaven, filled all the Earth with infinite light.

poems.title: Book I, 80: On John the Apostle
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: John the Divine high-priest of Ephesus, was the first who said from God that the Word was God.

poems.title: Book I, 81: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: John first heard the Word speak and himself said that the Word was God.

poems.title: Book I, 82: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: John, having reached the house of heavenly wisdom in which Ged is well pleased, said that the Word was God.

poems.title: Book I, 83: On Matthew
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Matthew wrote in his pages, after. leaving the house of the publican, all the high marvels of the Incarnation of God.

poems.title: Book I, 84: On Luke
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Luke wove skillfully into the vitals of the volume the deeds of Christ which brought about eternal life.

poems.title: Book I, 85: On Mark
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Night no longer covers the people of Egypt, as its name signifies, since it received the light of the voice of Mark.

poems.title: Book I, 86: On St. Basil
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Basil had for his lot the virginity and wisdom of John, having in this a like lot with Gregory.

poems.title: Book I, 87: On St. Polycarp
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is the merciful Polyearp who occupied a high priest’s throne, and won truly a martyr’s crown.

poems.title: Book I, 88: On St. Dionysius
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou who didst sing the hierarchic ranks of the heavenly companies and didst bring to light the mystic meaning of visible types, lightest the torch, pleasing to God, of oracles wise unto life.

poems.title: Book I, 89: On St. Nicholas
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Polycarp has Nicholas near him because the hands of both were ever most prompt to deeds of mercy.

poems.title: Book I, 90: On Cyrus and Joannes
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Ascribed to Sophronius Patriarch of Jerusalem.
poems.text: To the holy martyrs, Cyrus, a past master in the art of healing, and Joannes, did Sophronius, as a slight return for his escape from a soul-distressing complaint of the eyes, dedicate this book.

poems.title: Book I, 91: On the Emperor Justinian, in Ephesus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: By the command of Christ did John crown Justinian and admirable Theodora.

poems.title: Book I, 94: On the Death of the Holy Virgin
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The disciples, their hearts uplifted by the divine command, came calling to each other in glittering robes to the house of the immaculate and blameless woman, some from the East, some from the West, others from the South, and others came from the North, seeking to inter the body of Her, the world’s saviour.

poems.title: Book I, 95: In Ephesus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: To thee, O blessed one, from thee, I give the spoils thou gavest me in war.

poems.title: Book I, 96: On a Sceptre
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Worthy Amantius obtained this dignity, because he was faithful to the Emperor and delighted Christ by his fear of God.

poems.title: Book I, 97: In Melite
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I am the celebrated temple of the Emperor Justin. The Consul Theodorus, the strong, thrice a Prefect, dedicated me to the Emperor and his son Justinian, the general of the whole army.

poems.title: Book I, 98: In the same Place
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou seest the famous work of the Emperor Justin and of Justinian, the mighty general, glittering with the lustre of vast store of minerals. This was made by famous Theodorus, who, glorifying the city, thrice protected it by his consular office.

poems.title: Book I, 99: On the Pillar of Holy Daniel on the Bosphorus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Midmost of earth and heaven stands a man, dreading not the winds that blow from all quarters . . . both feet firmly planted on the column. He is nourished by ambrosial hunger and painless thirst, ever preaching the Son of the Immaculate Mother.

poems.title: Book I, 100: On Nilus the Great Hermit
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The stream of the river Nile can water the earth and the word of the monk Nilus can delight the mind.

poems.title: Book I, 102: On our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ the Son of God
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: O Tuov who art beyond all things (for how can I celebrate Thee more), how shall I tell Thy name Who art supreme above all ? How shall I sing Thee in words, Whom no words can comprehend ?

poems.title: Book I, 103: On the Lintel of a House in Cyzicus which was saved from Fire
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Bloodthirsty Momus, thy own bitter arrow slew thee, for God delivered me, this wealthy house, from thy fury.

poems.title: Book I, 104: On the Chest containing the Relics of the Holy Martyr Acacius and of King Alexander
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Here lie the bodies, discovered one happy day, of the Martyr Acacius and the priest Alexander.

poems.title: Book I, 105: On Eudocia the Wife of King Theodosius
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The wise mistress of the world, inflamed by pious love, cometh as a servant, and she who is worshipped by all mankind worshippeth the tomb of One. For He who gave her a husband and a throne, died as a Man but lives a God. Below He played the man, but above He was as He was.

poems.title: Book I, 106: In the Golden Hall of Mazarinus (after the Restoration of Images)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The light of Truth hath shone forth again, and blunts the eyes of the false teachers. Piety hath increased and Error is fallen; Faith flourisheth and Grace groweth. For behold, Christ pictured again shines above the imperial throne and overthrows the dark heresies. And above the entrance, like a holy door, is imaged the guardian Virgin. The Emperor and the Patriarch, as victorious over Error, are pictured near with their fellow-workers, and all around, as sentries of the house, are angels, disciples, martyrs, priests: whence we call this now the Christotriclinium (the hall of Christ) instead of by its former name Chrysotriclinium (the Golden Hall), since it has the throne of the Lord Christ and of his Mother, and the images of the Apostles and of Michael, author of wisdom.

poems.title: Book I, 107: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: O Emperor Michael, as preserving the bright preciousness of the ancient image, and as conqueror of all fleshly stains, thou dost picture the Lord in colours too, establishing by deed the word of dogma.

poems.title: Book I, 108: On Adam (Anonymous)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Not without wisdom was Adam so called, for the four letters represent the four quarters of the earth. The Alpha he has from Anatolé (the East), the Delta from Dysis (the West), the second Alpha is from Arctus (the North) and the Mu from Mesembria (the South).

poems.title: Book I, 109: In the Church of the Holy Virgin at the Fountain
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Ascribed to Ignatius the Magister Grammaticorum.
poems.text: Basil, Leo, and Constantine redecorate the ruined church of the Virgin.

poems.title: Book I, 110: In the same Church on the picture of the Ascension in the Dome
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Ascribed to Ignatius the Magister Grammaticorum.
poems.text: Ascending from Earth, O Saviour, to Thy Father’s throne, Thou showest Thy Mother's house to be a spiritual source of higher gifts.

poems.title: Book I, 111: In the same Church on the Crucifixion
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Ascribed to Ignatius the Magister Grammaticorum.
poems.text: Dead Hell vomits up the dead, being purged by the flesh of the Lord.

poems.title: Book I, 112: In the same Church on the Transfiguration
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Ascribed to Ignatius the Magister Grammaticorum.
poems.text: Christ on Tabor, shining brighter than light, hath done away with the shadow of the old Law.

poems.title: Book I, 113: In the same Church on the Presentation
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Ascribed to Ignatius the Magister Grammaticorum.
poems.text: The Boy now seen in the old man’s arms is the ancient Creator of Time.

poems.title: Book I, 114: In the same Church on the Salutation
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Ascribed to Ignatius the Magister Grammaticorum.
poems.text: The Lord saying “Hail” to the women presages the salvation of the world.

poems.title: Book I, 115: On the Virgin
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A Virgin bore a Son; after a Son she was a Virgin.

poems.title: Book I, 116: On the Saviour
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Blessed Curist, immortal Light of men, Son of God, receive gifts of crystal and sardonyx, incorruptible Son of a Virgin, Son of God, gifts of crystal and sardonyx.

poems.title: Book I, 117: On the Blind Man
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The blind, whose eyes were closed from birth, saw ; for Christ came, the Grace that is all eyes.

poems.title: Book I, 118: Prayers
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Our wicked enemy raised a tempest of passions, rousing the sea with his winds; whence he tosses and submerges and floods the cargo of our ship the soul. But, do thou, O Christ, calm and stiller of tempest, anchoring us safely in thy harbour, show our sins dry and this our enemy soaked with disaster.

poems.title: Book I, 119: The Argument, an eloquent Apology, of a Homeric Cento
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The book of Patricius, the God-fearing priest, who performed a great task, composing from the works of Homer a glorious song of splendid verses, announcing the deeds of the invincible God ; how He came to the company of men and took human form, and was hidden when an infant in the blameless womb of a Virgin, He whom the infinite universe cannot hold ; and how He sucked from the breast of the Virgin, once great with child from God, the stream of maiden milk it spouted; how Herod, in his folly seeking the death of the immortal God, slew the still tender babes ; how John washed Him in the waters of the river; how He took to Him His twelve excellent companions; the limbs of how many He made whole, driving out loathly diseases, and darkness of sight, and how He stayed the running stream of blood in the weeping woman who touched His raiment ; and how many victims of the cruel fates He brought back to the light from the dark pit ; and how He left us memorials of His holy Passion ; how by the hands of men He was tortured by cruel bonds, by His own will, for no mortal man could war with God who ruleth on high, unless He Himself decreed it; how He died and burst the iron gates of Hell and led thence into Heaven by the immaculate commnand of His Father the faithful spirits, having arisen on the third morn, the primal offspring of the Father who hath no beginning.

poems.title: Book I, 120: In Blachernae, in the Church of the Virgin
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: If thou seekest the dread throne of God on Earth, marvel as thou gazest on the house of the Virgin. For she who beareth God in her arms, beareth Him to the glory of this place. Here they who are set up to rule over the Earth believe that their sceptres are rendered victorious. Here the Patriarch, ever wakeful, averts many catastrophes in the world. The barbarians, attacking the city, on only seeing Her at the head of the army bent at once their stubborn necks.

poems.title: Book I, 121: In the same Church
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The house of the Virgin, like her Son, was destined to become a second gate of God. An ark hath appeared holier than that of old, not containing the tables written by God’s hand but having received within it God himself. Here are fountains of purification from the flesh, here is redemption of errors of the soul. There is no evil circumstance, but from Her gusheth a miraculous gift to cure it. Here, when She overthrew the foe, She destroyed them by water, not by the spear. She hath not one method of defeat alone, who bore Christ and putteth the barbarians to flight.

poems.title: Book I, 122: On the Virgin and Child
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is she who bore a child and remained a Virgin. Wonder not thereat, for the Child is God, who consented to put on flesh.

poems.title: Book I, 123: On the Rock of Calvary
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thrice-Blessed rock, who didst receive the blood that issued from God, the fiery children of Heaven guard thee around, and Kings, inhabitants of the Earth, sing thy praise.

poems.title: Book III, 1: On Dionysus conducting his mother Semele to Heaven, preceded by Hermes, Satyrs, and Sileni escorting them with Torches
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The fair-haired daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, slain in childbirth by the bolt of Zeus, is being led up from Acheron by her son Dionysus, the thyrsuslover, who avengeth the godless insolence of Pentheus.

poems.title: Book III, 2: Telephus recognised by his Mother
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Leaving the valleys of Arcadia because of my mother Auge, I Telephus, myself the dear son of Heracles, set foot on this Teuthranian land, that I might bring her back to Arcadia.

poems.title: Book III, 3: Phoenix blinded by his father Amyntor, whom his own wife Alcimede attempts to restrain
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Alcimede is holding back her husband Amyntor from their son Phoenix, wishing to appease his father’s wrath. He quarrelled with his father for his virtuous mother’s sake, because he desired to lie with a slave concubine. His father, listening to crafty whispered slander, was wrath with the young man, and approached him with a torch to burn out his eyes.

poems.title: Book III, 4: Polymedes and Clylius, the sons of Phineus the Thracian, who slew their father’s Phrygian wife, because he took her to wife while still married to their mother Cleopatra
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Clytius and Polymedes, renowned for wisdom, are slaying their Phrygian stepmother for their own mother’s sake. Cleopatra therefore is glad of heart, having seen the wife of Phineus justly slain.

poems.title: Book III, 5: Cresphontes is killing Polyphontes, the slayer of his father ; Merope is there holding a staff and helping her son to slay him
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou didst formerly slay, O Polyphontes, the father of Cresphontes, desiring to defile the bed of his wedded wife. And long after came his son to avenge his father’s murder, and slew thee for the sake of his mother Merope. Therefore hath he planted his spear in thy back, and she is helping, striking thee on the forehead with a heavy staff.

poems.title: Book III, 6: The Pytho slain by Apollo and Artemis, because it appeared and prevented Leto from approaching the oracle at Delphi which she went to occupy
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Leto in utter loathing is turning away from the earthborn Pytho, a creeping thing, all confusedly coiled ; for it wishes to annoy the wise goddess: but Phoebus, shooting from the height, lays it low in its blood. He shall make the Delphian tripod inspired, but the Pytho shall yield up its life with groans and bitter hisses.

poems.title: Book III, 7: On the North Side: The story of Zethus and Amphion
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Amphion and Zethus, scions of Zeus, slay this woman Dirce, the injurer of your mother Antiope, whom formerly she kept in prison owing to her jealous spite, but whom she now beseeches with tears. Attach her to the bull with a double rope, that it may drag her body through this thicket.

poems.title: Book III, 8: Ulysses in Hades questioning his mother Anticlea concerning affairs at home
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Anticlea, mother of wise Ulysses, thou didst not live to receive thy son in Ithaca; but now he marvelleth, seeing thee, his sweet mother, on the shore of Acheron.

poems.title: Book III, 9: Pelias and Neleus, the sons of Poseidon, delivering from bonds their mother Tyro, whom her father Salmoneus imprisoned owing to her seduction, and whom her step-mother Sidero tortured
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Let not the bonds of Sidero torment thee any longer, Tyro, crouching before this thy father, Salmoneus; for he shall not keep thee in bondage longer, now he sees Neleus and Pelias approach to restrain him.

poems.title: Book III, 10: On the West Side: The recognition of Eunous and Thoas, the children of Hypsipyle, by their mother
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Show, Thoas, this plant of Bacchus, for so shalt thou save from death thy mother, the slave Hypsipyle, who suffered from the wrath of Eurydice, since the earth-born snake slew Archemorus. And go thou too, Eunous, leaving the borders of the Asopian land, to take thy mother to pleasant Lemnos.

poems.title: Book III, 11: Polydectes the King of Seriphus being turned into stone by Perseus with the Gorgon’s head
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou didst dare, Polydectes, to defile the bed of Danae, succeeding Zeus in unholy wedlock. Therefore, Perseus here uncovered the Gorgon’s eyes and made thy limbs stone, to do pleasure to his mother.

poems.title: Book III, 12: Ixion killing Phorbas and Polymelus, for their murder of his mother Megara
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Ixion, whom you see, laid low Phorbas and Pelymelus, taking vengeance on them for their vengeance on his mother.

poems.title: Book III, 13: Heracles leading his mother Alcmene to the Elysian Plains to wed her to Rhadamanthys, and his own reception into the number of the gods
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Bold Heracles gave this his mother Alemene in holy wedlock to Rhadamanthys.

poems.title: Book III, 14: Tityus shot down by Apollo and Artemis for daring to assault their mother Leto
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Lustful and drunk with folly, why didst thou try to force the bride of Zeus, who now, as thou deservedst, bathed thee in blood and left thee righteously on the ground, food for beasts and birds.

poems.title: Book III, 15: Bellerophon saved by his son Glaucus, when having fallen from the back of Pegasus into the Aleian plain he was about to be killed by Megapenthes, the son of Proetus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: No longer could Bellerophon stay the murderous hand of this son of Proetus, nor the death designed for him by his father. Glaucus, in vain thou fearest for him (?); he shall escape the plot of Iobates, for thus the Destinies decreed. Thyself, too, then didst shield thy father from death, standing near him, and wast an observant witness to the truth of the glorious story.

poems.title: Book III, 16: At the door of the temple as we approach it are Aeolus and Boeotus, the sons of Poseidon, delivering their mother Melanippe from the fetters in which she was placed by her father owing to her seduction
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Aeolus and Boeotus, a clever and pious task ye performed in saving your mother from death. Therefore ye were proved to be brave men, one of you from Aeolis, the other from Boeotia.

poems.title: Book III, 18: Cleobis and Biton, who enabled their mother Cydippe, the priestess of Hera at Argos, to sacrifice, by putting their own necks under the yoke, when the oxen delayed
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This story of Cydippe and her sons’ piety is not false, but has the beauty of truth. A delightful labour and a seasonable for men was theirs ; they undertook a glorious task out of piety to their mother. Rejoice even among the dead ye men famous for your piety and may you alone have age-long story.

poems.title: Book III, 19: Romulus and Remus deliver their mother Servilia from the cruelty of Amulius
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou didst bear secretly this offspring to Ares, Romulus and Remus, at one birth. A she-wolf brought them up in a cave, and they delivered thee by force from woe ill to cure.

poems.title: Book V, 1: Proem of Constantine Cephalas
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Warming the hearts of youth with learned fervour, I will make Love the beginning of my discourse, for it is he who lighteth the torch for youth,

poems.title: Book V, 2
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: She who sets the town on fire, Sthenelais, the high-priced whore, whose breath smells of gold for those who desire her, lay by me naked in my dream all night long until the sweet dawn, giving herself to me for nothing. No longer shall I implore the cruel beauty, nor mourn for myself, now I have Sleep to grant me what he granted.

poems.title: Book V, 5
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: To faithless Nape Flaccus gave myself, this silver lamp, the faithful confidant of the loves of the night ; and now I droop at her bedside, looking on the lewdness of the forsworn girl. But thou, Flaccus, liest awake, tormented by cruel care, and both of us are burning far away from each other.

poems.title: Book V, 11
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Cypris, if thou savest those at sea, save me, beloved goddess, who perish ship-wrecked on land.

poems.title: Book V, 20
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I neither wish to marry a young girl nor an old woman. The one I pity, the other I revere. Neither sour grape nor raisin would I have, but a beauty ripe for the chamber of Love.

poems.title: Book V, 26
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Whether I see thee, my queen, with glossy raven locks, or again with fair hair, the same charm illumines thy head. Verily Love shall lodge still in this hair when it is grey.

poems.title: Book V, 29
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Sweet is fruition, who denies it? but when it demands money it becomes bitterer than hellebore.

poems.title: Book V, 33
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou didst fall in rain of gold on Danae, Olympian Zeus, that the child might yield to thee as to a gift, and not tremble before thee as before a god.

poems.title: Book V, 34
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Zeus bought Danae for gold, and I buy you for a gold coin. I can’t give more than Zeus did.

poems.title: Book V, 45
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A young girl increases her little store not by her art, but by her nature.

poems.title: Book V, 50
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Poverty and Love are my two woes. Poverty I will bear easily, but the fire of Cypris I cannot.

poems.title: Book V, 51
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I fell in love, I kissed, I was favoured, I enjoyed, I am loved; but who am I, and who is she, and how it befel, Cypris alone knows.

poems.title: Book V, 65
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Zeus came as an eagle to god-like Ganymede, as a swan came he to the fair-haired mother of Helen. So there is no comparison between the two things ; one person likes one, another likes the other; I like both.

poems.title: Book V, 67
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Beauty without charm only pleases us, but does not hold us; it is like a bait floating without a hook.

poems.title: Book V, 68
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Ascribed to Lucilius or Polemo of Pontus.
poems.text: Either put an entire stop to loving, Eros, or else add being loved, so that you may either abolish desire or temper it.

poems.title: Book V, 82
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Proud waitress of the bath, why dost thou bathe me so fiercely? Before I have stripped I feel the fire. ;

poems.title: Book V, 83
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Oh, would I were the wind, that walking on the shore thou mightest bare thy bosom and take me to thee as I blow.

poems.title: Book V, 84
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Oh, would I were a pink rose, that thy hand might pluck me to give to thy snowy breasts.

poems.title: Book V, 86
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Have mercy on me, dear Phoebus; for thou, drawer of the swift bow, wast wounded by the swift arrows of Love.

poems.title: Book V, 90
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I senp thee sweet perfume, ministering to scent with scent, even as one who to Bacchus offers the flowing gift of Bacchus.

poems.title: Book V, 91
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I senp thee sweet perfume, not so much honouring thee as it ; for thou canst perfume the perfume.

poems.title: Book V, 95
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Four are the Graces, there are two Aphrodites and ten Muses. Dercylis is one of all, a Grace, an Aphrodite, and a Muse.

poems.title: Book V, 98
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Prepare thy bow, Cypris, and find at thy leisure another target; for I have no room at all left fora wound.

poems.title: Book V, 100
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: If anyone blame me because, a skilled servant of Love, I go to the chase, my eyes armed with birdlime to catch ladies, let him know that Zeus and Hades and the Lord of the Sea were slaves of violent desire. If the gods are such and they bid men follow their example, what wrong do I do in learning their deeds?

poems.title: Book V, 101
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: He. Good day, my dear. She. Good day. He. Who is she who is walking in front of you? She. What is that to you? He. I have a reason for asking. She. My mistress. He. May I hope? She. What do you want? He. A night. She. What have you for her? He. Gold. She. Then take heart. He. So much (shening the amount), She. You can't.

poems.title: Book V, 122
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Son of illustrious Megistocles, I beseech thee, not even though he seem to thee more precious than thy two eyes, though he be glowing from the bath of the Graces, hum not around the lovely boy. Neither gentle nor simple-hearted is he, but courted by many, and no novice inlove. Beware, my friend, and fan not the flame.

poems.title: Book V, 135: To his Jug
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Round, well-moulded, one-eared, long-necked, babbling with thy little mouth, merry waitress of Bacchus and the Muses and Cytherea, sweetly-laughing treasuress of our club, why when I am sober are you full and when I get tipsy do you become sober? You don’t keep the laws of conviviality.

poems.title: Book V, 142
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Which is it? is the garland the rose of Dionysius, or is he the garland’s rose? I think the garland is less lovely.

poems.title: Book V, 161
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Euphro, Thais and Boidion, Diomede’s old women, the twenty-oared transports of ship-captains, have east ashore, one apiece, naked and worse off than shipwrecked mariners, Agis, Cleophon and Antagoras. But fly from Aphrodite’s corsairs and their ships ; they are worse foes than the Sirens.

poems.title: Book V, 168
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Hurl fire and snow upon me, and if thou wilt, strike me with thy bolt, or sweep me to the cliffs or to the deep. For he who is worn out by battle with Desire and utterly overcome by Love, feels not even the blast of Jove’s fire.

poems.title: Book V, 194
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The Loves themselves escorted soft Irene as she issued from the golden chamber of Cypris, a holy flower of beauty from head to fovt, as though carved of white marble, laden with virgin graces. Full many an arrow to a young man’s heart did they let fly from their purple bow-strings.

poems.title: Book V, 200
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The saffron robe of Alexo, and her dark green ivy crown, still smelling of myrrh, with her snood she dedicates to sweet Priapus with the effeminate melting eyes, in memory of his holy night-festival.

poems.title: Book V, 201
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Leontis lay awake till the lovely star of morn, taking her delight with golden Sthenius, and ever since that vigil it hangs here in the shrine of Cypris, the lyre the Muses helped her then to play.

poems.title: Book V, 202
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Piango dedicated on the portals of the equestrian god her purple whip and her polished reins, after winning as a jockey her race with Philaenis, her practised rival, when the horses of the evening had just begun to neigh. Dear Cypris, give her unquestioned glory for her victory, stablishing for her this favour not to be forgotten.

poems.title: Book V, 205
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Nico’s love-charm, that can compel a man to come from oversea and boys from their rooms, carved of transparent amethyst, set in gold and hung upon a soft thread of purple wool, she, the witch of Larissa presents to thee Cypris, to possess and treasure.

poems.title: Book V, 209
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: By thy strand, O Paphian Cytherea, Cleander saw Nico swimming in the blue sea, and burning with love he teok to his heart dry coals from the wet maiden. He, standing on the land, was shipwrecked, but she in the sea was received gently by the beach. Now they are both equally in love, for the prayers were not in vain that he breathed on that strand.

poems.title: Book V, 242
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: When I saw Melite, I grew pale, for her husband was with her, but I said to her trembling, “May I push back the bolts of your door, loosening ‘the bolt-pin, and fixing in the middle the tip of my key pierce the damp base of the folding door?” But she, laughing and glancing at her husband, said, “You had better keep away from my door, or the dog may worry you.”

poems.title: Book V, 249
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: O naughty Rhodope, now yielding to the arrows of Cypris, and forswearing thy insufferable pride, you hold mein your arms by your bed, and I lie, it seems, in chains with no desire for liberty. Thus do souls and languid bodies meet, mingled by the streams of love.

poems.title: Book V, 251
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: You roll your eyes to express hidden fires and you grimace, twisting and protruding your reddened lips ; you giggle constantly and shake the glory of your curls, and your haughty hands, I see, are stretched out in despair. But your disdainful heart is not bent, and even in your decline you are not softened.

poems.title: Book V, 253
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Way, Chrysilla, do you bend your head and gaze at the floor, and why do your fingers trifle with your girdle’s knot? Shame mates not with Cypris, and if you must be silent, by some sign at least tell me that you submit to the Paphian goddess,

poems.title: Book V, 265
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Phyllis sent her eyes to sea to seek Demophoon, but his oath he had flung to the winds and he was false to her. Now, dear, I thy Demophoon keep my tryst to thee on the sea-shore; but how is it, Phyllis, that thou are false?

poems.title: Book V, 277
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Let males be for others. I can love but women, whose charms are more enduring. There is no beauty in youths at the age of puberty; I hate the unkind hair that begins to grow too soon.

poems.title: Book V, 284
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I Love everything in you. I hate only your undiscerning eye which is pleased by odious men.

poems.title: Book V, 295
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Touch, O cup, the lips that drop honey, suck now thou hast the chance. I envy not, but would thy luck were mine.

poems.title: Book V, 303
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Tuere is a noise of loud shouting and great tumult in the street, and why takest thou no heed, Cypris? It is thy boy arrested on his way by all who have the fire of love in their hearts.

poems.title: Book V, 304
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: When you were a green grape you refused me, when you were ripe you bade me be off, at least grudge me not a little of your raisin.

poems.title: Book V, 305
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A girl kissed me in the evening with wet lips. The kiss was nectar, for her mouth smelt sweet of nectar; and I am drunk with the kiss, I have drunk love in abundance.

poems.title: Book V, 308
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: O you pretty creature, wait for me. What is your name? Where can I see you? I will give what you choose. You don’t even speak. Where do you live? I will send someone with you. Do you possibly belong to anyone? Well, you stuck-up thing, goodbye. You won’t even say “goodbye.” But again and again I willaccost you. I know how to soften even more hard-hearted beauties ; and for the present, ‘‘ goodbye, madam !”’

poems.title: Book V, 309
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Love may justly be called thrice a brigand. He is wakeful, reckless, and he strips us bare.

poems.title: Book VI, 3
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Heracles, who treadest stony Trachis and Oeta and the headland of Pholoe clothed in deep forest, to thee Dionysius offers this club yet green, which he cut himself with his sickle from a wild olive-tree.

poems.title: Book VI, 6: On a Caldron in Delphi
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Amphitryon dedicated me, having won me from the Teleboi.

poems.title: Book VI, 7: On Another
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Scarus, having conquered in the boxing contest, dedicated me a beautiful ornament to thee, Apollo the Far-shooter.

poems.title: Book VI, 8: On Another
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Laodamas himself during his reign dedicated to thee, Apollo the Archer, this tripod as a beautiful ornament.

poems.title: Book VI, 10
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Trito-born, Saviour, daughter of Zeus, who hatest wedlock, Pallas, queen of childless virginity, Seleucus built thee this horned altar at the bidding of Apollo.

poems.title: Book VI, 11
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The three brothers, skilled in three crafts, dedicate to Pan, Damis the huntsman this long net, Pigres his light-meshed fowling net, and Clitor, the nightrower, his tunic for red mullet. Look kindly on the pious brethren, O Pan, and grant them gain from fowl, fish and venison.

poems.title: Book VI, 21
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: To thee, Priapus the gardener, did Potamon, who gained wealth by this calling, dedicate the hoe that dug his thirsty garden, and his curved sickle for cutting vegetables, the ragged cloak that kept the rain off his back, his strong boots of untanned hide, the dibble for planting out young cabbages going straight into the easily pierced soil, and his mattock that never ceased during the dry summer to refresh the thirsty beds with draughts from the channels.

poems.title: Book VI, 22
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The fruit-watcher dedicated to rustic Priapus, carved out of a trunk, this sacrifice from the trees, a newly split pomegranate, this quince covered with fresh down, a navelled fig with wrinkled skin, a purple cluster of thick-set grapes, fountain of wine, and a walnut just out of its green rind.

poems.title: Book VI, 23
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Hermes, who dwellest in this wave-beaten rock-cave, that gives good footing to fisher gulls, accept this fragment of the great seine worn by the sea and scraped often by the rough beach; this little purse-seine, the round weel that entraps fishes, the float whose task it is to mark where the weels are concealed, and the long cane rod, the child of the marsh, with its horse-hair line, not unfurnished with hooks, wound round it.

poems.title: Book VI, 24
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Hetroporus dedicates to the Syrian Goddess in the porch of this temple his net worn out in vain. It is untainted byany catch of fish, but he hauled out plenty of sea-weed in it on the spacious beach of the anchorage.

poems.title: Book VI, 37
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The rustic herdsmen cut on the mountain this beech-branch which old age had bent as it bends us, and having trimmed it, set it up by the road, a pretty toy for Pan who protects the glossy cattle.

poems.title: Book VI, 42
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Poor Alcimenes, having tasted the gifts of fruitful summer in a little garden, when he brought to Pan as a present an apple, a fig, and some water, said: “Thou givest me from thy treasury the good things of life; so accept these, the fruits from the garden and the water from thy rock, and give me in return more than thou hast received.”

poems.title: Book VI, 45
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Comautus hung up alive to Bacchus this hedgehog, its body bristling with sharp spines, the grapegatherer, the spoiler of the sweet vineyards, having caught it curled up in a ball and rolling on the grapes.

poems.title: Book VI, 48
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Bitto dedicated to Athene her industrious loumcomb, the implement of her scanty livelihood, for then she conceived a hatred for all toil among workfolk, and for the weaver’s wretched cares. To Athene she said, “I will take to the works of Cypris, voting like Paris against thee.”

poems.title: Book VI, 49: On a Tripod at Delphi
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I am a bronze tripod, dedicated at Delphi to adorn the shrine ; swift-footed Achilles offered me as a prize at Patroclus’ funeral feast, and Diomed the warlike son of Tydeus dedicated me, having conquered in the horse-race by the broad Hellespont.

poems.title: Book VI, 51
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: To thee, my mother Rhea, nurse of Phrygian lions, whose devotees tread the heights of Dindymus, did womanish Alexis, ceasing from furious clashing of the brass, dedicate these stimulants of his madness— his shrill-toned cymbals, the noise of his deep-voiced flute, to which the crooked horn of a young steer gave a curved form, his echoing tambourines, his knives reddened with blood, and the yellow hair which once tossed on his shoulders. Be kind, O Queen, and give rest in his old age from his former wildness to him who went mad in his youth.

poems.title: Book VI, 58
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Ascribed to Isidorus Scholasticus of Bolbytine.
poems.text: Thy friend Endymion, Moon, dedicates to thee, ashamed, his bed that survives in vain and its futile cover; for grey hair reigns over his whole head and no trace of his former beauty is left.

poems.title: Book VI, 77
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Xenophon, the toper, dedicates his empty cask to thee, Bacchus. Receive it kindly, for it is all he has.

poems.title: Book VI, 78
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Daphnis, lover of women, dedicates to dear Pan the pierced reed-pipe, and this skin and club. Accept O Pan, the gifts of Daphnis, for like him thou lovest music and art unhappy in love.

poems.title: Book VI, 87
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thy Pan, Bacchus, dedicates to thee his fawn-skin and club, seduced away from thy dance by Venus ; for he loves Echo and wanders up and down. But do thou, Bacchus, forgive him, for the like hath befallen thee.

poems.title: Book VI, 88
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Cytherea herself loosed from her breast her delightful cestus and gave it to thee, Ino, for thine own, so that ever with love-charms that melt the heart thou mayest subdue men; and surely thou hast spent them all on me alone.

poems.title: Book VI, 96
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Glaucon and Corydon, who keep their cattle on the hills, Arcadians both, drawing back its neck slaughtered for Cyllenian Pan, the mountain-lover, a horned steer, and fixed by a long naii to the goodly plane-tree its horns, twelve palms long, a fair ornament for the pastoral god.

poems.title: Book VI, 109
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Crauais the huntsman, son of Neolaidas, an Arcadian of Orchomenus, gives to thee, Pan the Scout, this scrap of his old fowling-net, his triple-twisted snare for the feet, his spring-traps made of sinews, his latticed cages, his nooses for the throat which one draws up, his sharp stakes hardened in the fire, the sticky moisture of the oak, the cane wet with it that catches birds, the triple cord which is pulled to close the hidden spring-net, and the net for catching by the neck the clamorous cranes.

poems.title: Book VI, 110
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Cleotaus killed with his sharp spear, from his ambush under the hill, this hind by the winding water of Maeander, and nailed to the lofty pine the eight-tyned defence of its forehead.

poems.title: Book VI, 111
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Lycormas, the son of Thearidas of Lasion, slew with the butt end of his whirled spear the hind that used to feed about the Ladon and the waters of Erymanthus and the heights of Pholoe, home of wild beasts. Its skin and two spiked horns he flenched, and hung up by the shrine of Artemis the Huntress.

poems.title: Book VI, 115
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The bull that bellowed erst on the heights of Orbelus, the brute that laid Macedonia waste, Philip, the wielder of the thunder-bolt, the destroyer of the Dardanians, hath slain, piercing its forehead with his hunting-spear; and to thee, Heracles, he hath dedicated with its strong hide these horns, the defence of its monstrous head. From thy race he sprung, and it well becomes him to emulate his ancestor's prowess in slaying cattle.

poems.title: Book VI, 117
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The hammer from the fire, with the pliers and tongs, is consecrated to thee, Hephaestus, the gift of Polyerates, with which often beating on his anvil he gained substance for his children, driving away doleful poverty.

poems.title: Book VI, 118
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The lyre, the bow, and the intricate nets are dedicated to Phoebus by Sosis, Phila and Polycrates. The archer dedicated the horn bow, she, the musician, the tortoise-shell lyre, the hunter his nets. Let the first be supreme in archery, let her be supreme in playing, and let the last be first among huntsmen.

poems.title: Book VI, 151
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Miccus of Pellene hung in the temple of Ilian Athene this deep-toned flute of Ares, the Tyrrhenian instrument by which he formerly uttered many a loud message of peace or war.

poems.title: Book VI, 154
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Ascribed to Leonidas of Tarentum or Gaetulicus.
poems.text: Old Biton of Arcady dedicated these things to rustic Pan, and Bacchus the reveller, and the Nymphs; to Pan a newly born kid, its mother’s play-fellow, to Bacchus a branch of vagrant ivy, to the Nymphs the varied bloom of shady Autumn and blood-red roses in full flower. In return for which, bless the old man’s house with abundance— ye Nymphs, of water, Pan, of milk, and Bacchus, of grapes.

poems.title: Book VI, 158: An Exercise on the Theme of No. 154
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A triple gift did Biton dedicate under the greenwood tree, to Pan a goat, roses to the Nymphs, and a thyrsus to Bacchus. Receive with joy his gifts, ye gods, and increase, Pan, his flock, ye Nymphs his fountain, and Bacchus his cellar.

poems.title: Book VI, 165
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Evanthe, when she transferred her hand from the unsteady service of the thyrsus to the steady service of the wine-cup, dedicated to Bacchus her whirling tambourine that stirs the rout of the Bacchants to fury, this dappled spoil of a flayed fawn, her clashing brass corybantic cymbals, her green thyrsus surmounted by a pine-cone, her light, but deeply-booming drum, and the winnowing-basket she often carried raised above her snooded hair.

poems.title: Book VI, 169
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Comautus, seeing the porcupine carrying grapes on its spines, slew it in this vineyard, and having dried it, he dedicated to Dionysus, who loves untempered wine, the spoiler of Dionysus’ gift.

poems.title: Book VI, 170
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The elms, and these lofty willows, and the holy spreading plane, and the springs, and these shepherds’ cups that cure fell thirst, are dedicate to Pan.

poems.title: Book VI, 171
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: To thy very self, O Sun, did the people of Dorian Rhodes raise high to heaven this colossus, then, when having laid to rest the brazen wave of war, they crowned their country with the spoils of their foes. Not only over the sea, but on the land, too, did they establish the lovely light of unfettered freedom. For to those who spring from the race of Heracles dominion is a heritage both on land and sea.

poems.title: Book VI, 172
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Cnidian Porpuyris suspends before thy chamber, Dionysus, these gauds of her beauty and her madness, her crowns, and this double thyrsus-spear, and her anklet, with all of which she raved her fill whenever she betook her to Dionysus, her ivy-decked fawn-skin knotted on her bosom.

poems.title: Book VI, 174
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The three girls all of an age, as clever as the spider at weaving delicate webs, dedicated here to Pallas, Demo her well-plaited basket, Arsinoe her spindle that produces the fine thread, and Bacchylis her well-wrought comb, the weaver’s nightingale, with the skilled stroke of which she deftly parted the threads. For each of them, stranger, willed to live without reproach, gaining her living by her hands.

poems.title: Book VI, 177
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: White-skinned Daphnis, who plays on his pretty pipe rustic airs, dedicated to Pan his pierced reed-pipe, his hare-club, his sharp spear, his fawnskin and the leather bag in which he used to carry apples.

poems.title: Book VI, 182
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Pigres dedicates to thee, Pan, his nets for birds, Damis his for mountain beasts, and Cleitor his for those of the deep: a common gift from the brothers for their luck in the various kinds of chase to thee who art skilled in the things of sea and land alike. In return for which, and recognising their piety, give one dominion in the sea, the other in the air, the third in the woods.

poems.title: Book VI, 183
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The hunter brothers suspended these nets to thee, Pan, gifts from three sorts of chase; Pigres from fowls, Cleitor from the sea, and Damis, the crafty tracker, from the land. But do thou reward their toil with success in wood, sea, and air.

poems.title: Book VI, 184
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The three huntsmen, each from a different craft, dedicated these nets in Pan’s temple; Pigres who set his nets for birds, Cleitor who set his for sea-fishes, and Damis who set his for the beasts of the waste. Therefore, Pan, make them more successful, the one in the air, the other in the thicket, and the third on the beach.

poems.title: Book VI, 185
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This heavy net for forest beasts did Damis dedicate, Pigres his light net that brings death to birds, and Cleitor his simple sweep-net woven of thread for the sea, praying all three to Pan the hunter’s god. Therefore, Pan, grant to strong Damis good booty of beasts, to Pigres of fowls, and to Cleitor of fishes.

poems.title: Book VI, 186
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: We three brothers of one house have dedicated three nets to thee, Pan, from mountain, air, and sea. Cast his nets for this one by the shingly beach, strike the game for this one in the woods, the home of wild beasts, and look with favour on the third among the birds; for thou hast gifts, kind god, from all our netting.

poems.title: Book VI, 187
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The holy triad of brothers dedicate to Pan each a token of his own craft; Pigres a portion from his birds, Cleitor from his fish, and Damis from his straight-cut stakes. In return for which grant to the one success by land, to the second by sea, and let the third win profit from the air.

poems.title: Book VI, 191
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Receive, Cypris, these gifts of Leonidas out of a poverty which is, as thou knowest, untempered but honest, these purple gleanings from the vine, this pickled olive, the prescribed sacrifice of barley-cake, a libation of wine which I strained off without shaking the vessel, and the sweet figs. Save me from want, as thou hast saved me from sickness, and then thou shalt see me sacrificing cattle. But hasten, goddess, to earn and receive my thanks.

poems.title: Book VI, 193
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Priapus of the beach, neighbour of the seaweed, Damoetas the fisherman, the fathomer of the deep, the very image of a sea-worn crag, the leech of the rocks, the sea-hunter, dedicates to thee this sweep-net, with which he comforted his old age.

poems.title: Book VI, 194: On a Trumpet
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Preserve, Tritonian goddess, the offerings and the offerer.

poems.title: Book VI, 196
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The bandy-legged, two-clawed sand-diver, the retrograde, neckless, eight-footed, the solid-backed, hard-skinned swimmer, the crab, does Copasus the line-fisher offer to Pan, as the first-fruits of his catch.

poems.title: Book VI, 203
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Ascribed to Lacon or Philippus of Thessalonica.
poems.text: The old lame serving-woman, hearing the good news of the healing water, came limping with an oaken staff that propped her stricken body. Pity seized the Nymphs who dwelt on the skirts of bellowing Etna in the watery house of their father, eddying Symaethus. The hot spring of Etna restored the strength of her lame legs, and to the Nymphs, who granted her prayer that they would send her back unsupported, she left her staff, and they rejoiced in the gift.

poems.title: Book VI, 208: It would seem on a Picture
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: She who brings the shoes is Menecratis, she with the cloak is Phemonoe, and Praxo she who holds the goblet. The temple and statue are Aphrodite’s. The offering is their joint one and it is the work of Aristomachus of the Strymonian land. They were all free-born courtesans, but chancing on more temperate love are now each the wife of one.

poems.title: Book VI, 209
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Bithynian Cythere dedicated me to thee, Cypris, according to her vow, the marble image of thy form. But do thou, as is thy wont, give her a great gift in return for this little one; she asks no more than that her husband may be of one heart and soul with her.

poems.title: Book VI, 210
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Now past her fiftieth year doth amorous Nicias hang in the fane of Cypris her sandals, locks of her uncoiled hair, her bronze mirror that lacketh not accuracy, her precious zone, and the things of which a man may not speak. But here you see the whole pageant of Cypris.

poems.title: Book VI, 219
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Goaded by the fury of the dreadful goddess, tossing his locks in wild frenzy, clothed in woman’s raiment with well-plaited tresses and a dainty netted hair-caul, a eunuch once took shelter in a mountain cavern, driven by the numbing snow of Zeus. But behind him rushed in unshivering a lion, slayer of bulls, returning to his den in the evening, who looking on the man, snuffing in his shapely nostrils the smell of human flesh, stood still on his sturdy feet, but rolling his eyes roared loudly from his greedy jaws. The cave, his den, thunders around him and the wooded peak that mounts nigh to the clouds echoes loud. But the priest startled by the deep voice felt all his stirred spirit broken in hisbreast. Yet he uttered from his lips the piercing shriek they use, and tossed his whirling locks, and holding up his great tambour, the revolving instrument of Olympian Rhea, he beat it, and it was the saviour of his life; for the lion hearing the unaccustomed hollow boom of the bull’s hide was afraid and took to flight. See how all-wise necessity taught a means of escape from death!

poems.title: Book VI, 223
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This mutilated body of a sea-wandering scolopendra eight fathoms long, all foul with foam and torn by the rocks, was found lying on this sandy beach by Hermonax when, in pursuit of his calling as a fisherman, he was drawing in his haul of fish, and having found it he hung it up as a gift to Ino and her son Palaemon, offering to the deities of the sea a monster of the sea.

poems.title: Book VI, 228
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Alcon did not lead to the bloody axe his labouring ox worn out by the furrows and old age, for he reverenced it for its service; and now somewhere in the deep meadow grass it lows rejoicing in its release from the plough.

poems.title: Book VI, 230
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: To thee, Phoebus of the cape, who rulest this fringe of the Bithynian land near the beach, did Damis the fisherman who ever rests his horn on the sand give this well protected trumpet-shell with its natural spikes, a humble present from a pious heart. The old man prays to thee that he may see death without disease.

poems.title: Book VI, 234
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The long-haired priest of Rhea, the newly gelded, the dancer from Lydian ‘Tmolus whose shriek is heard afar, dedicates, now he rests from his frenzy, to the solemn Mother who dwells by the banks of Sangarius these tambourines, his scourge armed with bones, these noisy brazen cymbals, and a scented lock of his hair.

poems.title: Book VI, 237
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The priest of Rhea dedicated to the mountain- Mother of the gods this raiment and these locks owing to an adventure such as this. As he was walking alone in the wood a savage lion met him and a struggle for his life was imminent. But the goddess put it in his mind to beat his tambourine and he made the ravening brute take flight, dreading the awful din. For this reason his locks hang from the whistling branches.

poems.title: Book VI, 241
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I, the helm, am graced by two gifts. I am lovely to look on for friends and a terror to foes. Piso? hath me from Pylaemenes. No other helmet was fit to sit on his head, no other head fit to wear me.
