poems.text: Marvellous is the art of the bull and man: he, the man, his limbs all tense, forces down by his might the savage beast. To bend back the sinews of its neck he grasps with his left hand its nostrils, with his right its horn, and shakes up the neck-bones. The beast, its neck subdued by his strong hands, sinks down on its hindquarters. One may fancy that in this bronze Art makes the beast breathe and bathes the man in sweat.

poems.title: Book XVI, 106: On a Statue of Capaneus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Had Capaneus been like this when he furiously attacked the towers of Thebes, contriving to mount through the air on a ladder, he would have taken the city by force in Fate’s despite; for even the bolt of Zeus would have deemed it shame to slay such a champion.

poems.title: Book XVI, 112: On a Bronze Statue of the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: My foe, more than the Greeks, was my maker, a second Odysseus, who put me in mind again of my evil, accursed hurt. They were not enough, the rock-cave, the rags, the pus, the sore, the misery, but he wrought in the brass even the pain.

poems.title: Book XVI, 115: On the Centaur Chiron
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A horse is shed forth from a man, and a man springs up from a horse; a man without feet and a swift horse without a head; a horse belches out a man, and a man farts out a horse.

poems.title: Book XVI, 120: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Attributed by Paton to Archelaus or Asclepiades.
poems.text: Lysippus modelled Alexander’s daring and his whole form. How great is the power of this bronze! The brazen king seems to be gazing at Zeus and about to say, “I set Earth under my feet; thyself, Zeus, possess Olympus.”

poems.title: Book XVI, 121: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Imagine that thou seest Alexander himself; so flash his very eyes in the bronze, so lives his dauntless mien. He alone subjected to the throne of Pella all the earth which the rays of Zeus look on from heaven.

poems.title: Book XVI, 122: On a Statue of the Same as a Child
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Here seest thou newly-born Alexander, the son of great-hearted Philip, him the bold-spirited to whom Olympias of old gave birth, to whom from his cradle Ares taught the labours of war and whom Fortune called to the throne.

poems.title: Book XVI, 123
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: No, by Heracles the ox-eater, ye country lads, no longer shall wily wolves set their feet here, and thieves shall refuse to tread the path of pilfering, even if the villagers lie in imprudent sleep. For Dionysius withal, not without a vow, hath set me, Heracles, here to be the place’s good defender.

poems.title: Book XVI, 124: On a Statue of Heracles
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Tremble not, traveller, at this, that I have unsheathed my bow and newly sharpened arrows and laid them at my feet, nor that I bear a club in my hand and wear round my shoulders the skin of a tawny lion. It is not my task to hurt all men, but only evil-doers, and I also can deliver the good from sorrow.

poems.title: Book XVI, 125: On a Picture of Ulysses
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Ever is the sea unkind to the son of Laertes; the flood hath bathed the picture and washed off the figure from the wood. What did it gain thereby? For in Homer’s verse the image of him is painted on immortal pages.

poems.title: Book XVI, 126: On the Minotaur
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The bull-boy, in no respect complete, he who betrays his mother’s passion, the man half-beast, the double nature, the bull-headed, the freak of bodies, who is neither a whole ox nor a whole man.

poems.title: Book XVI, 127
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Who moulded in bronze this one-shoed Thracian Lycurgus, the chieftain of the Edones? Look how, in his insolent fury, standing by the stem of Bacchus’ vine, he holds high over his head his heavy axe. His pose speaks of his old over-boldness, and even in the brass his insolent fury has that bitterness we look for.

poems.title: Book XVI, 129: On a Statue of Niobe
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: From a living being the gods made me a stone, but Praxiteles from a stone made me alive again.

poems.title: Book XVI, 135: On the Picture of Medea in Rome
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The art of Timomachus mingled the love and jealousy of Medea as she drags her children to death. She half consents as she looks at the sword, and half refuses, wishing both to save and to slay her children.

poems.title: Book XVI, 138: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Come, look on the child-murderess in a picture; look on her image, the Colchian’s, drawn by the hand of Timomachus. The sword is in her hand, great is her wrath, wild is her eye, the tears are falling for her most unhappy children. The painter has made a medley of all, uniting things most uncombinable, but he refrained from reddening his hand with blood.

poems.title: Book XVI, 140: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Come, look and marvel at the pity and wrath that dwell under her brow; look at the fiery orbs of her eyes; look at the mother’s hand, the hand of the bitterly suffering wife, drawn towards slaughter by a relenting impulse. The painter rightly hid from us the accomplishment of the murder, not wishing to blunt by mourning our admiration as we look on his work.

poems.title: Book XVI, 145: On a Statue of Ariadne
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: No mortal was thy sculptor, but he carved thee even as thy lover Bacchus saw thee reclining on the rock.

poems.title: Book XVI, 146: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Stranger, touch not this stone Ariadne, lest she leap up seeking Theseus.

poems.title: Book XVI, 151: On a Painting of Dido
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou seest, O stranger, the exact likeness of far-famed Dido, a portrait shining with divine beauty. Even so I was, but had not such a character as thou hearest, having gained glory rather for reputable things. For neither did I ever set eyes on Aeneas nor did I reach Libya at the time of the sack ot Troy, but to escape a forced marriage with Iarbas I plunged the two-edged sword into my heart. Ye Muses, why did ye arm chaste Virgil against me to slander thus falsely my virtue?

poems.title: Book XVI, 156: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: An Arcadian goddess am I, and I dwell by the portals of Dionysus, returning vocal responses. For no longer, dear Bacchus, do I hate thy companion. Come, Pan, let us talk in unison.

poems.title: Book XVI, 158
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Headed “Diotimus”; Paton does not say which Diotimus.
poems.text: I am Artemis fashioned in the form that befits me, and well does the brass itself tell that I am the daughter of Zeus and of no other. Consider the maiden’s audacity. Verily thou wouldst say that the whole earth is a hunting-ground too small for her.

poems.title: Book XVI, 159: On the Cnidian Aphrodite of Praxiteles
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Who gave a soul to marble? Who saw Cypris on earth? Who wrought such love-longing in a stone? This must be the work of Praxiteles’ hands, or else perchance Olympus is bereaved since the Paphian has descended to Cnidus.

poems.title: Book XVI, 162: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Cypris, seeing Cypris in Cnidus, said, “Alas alas where did Praxiteles see me naked?”

poems.title: Book XVI, 165: On the Cnidian Aphrodite
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Headed “Evenus”; Paton does not say which Evenus.
poems.text: Pallas and the consort of Zeus said, when they saw the Cnidian, “We are wrong in finding fault with Paris.”

poems.title: Book XVI, 166: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Headed “Evenus”; Paton does not say which Evenus.
poems.text: The neatherd alone saw of old on the mountains of Ida her who gained the prize of beauty, but Praxiteles has set her in full view of the Cnidians, having the vote of Paris to attest his skill.

poems.title: Book XVI, 168: On the Cnidian Aphrodite
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Paris, Anchises, and Adonis saw me naked. Those are all I know of, but how did Praxiteles contrive it?

poems.title: Book XVI, 169: On the Same and on the Athena in Athens
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Gaze from every side at the divine beauty of the foam-born Paphian and you will say, “I applaud the Phrygian’s judgment.” Again when you look at the Attic Pallas you will cry out, “It was just like a neatherd for Paris to pass her by.”

poems.title: Book XVI, 174: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Paris, seeing Cytherea in arms, said, “Cypris, wouldst thou that we went to the judgment so?” But she, with a gentle smile, answered, “Why should I lift up a shield in combat? If I conquer when naked, how will it be when I arm myself?”

poems.title: Book XVI, 175: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Headed “Antipater”; Paton does not say which Antipater.
poems.text: Either the stone statue, as being Aphrodite, armed itself, or perhaps rather Aphrodite saw the statue and swore, “Would I were it.”

poems.title: Book XVI, 176: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Headed “Antipater”; Paton does not say which Antipater.
poems.text: Cypris belongs to Sparta too, but her statue is not, as in other cities, draped in soft folds. No, on her head she wears a helmet instead of a veil, and bears a spear instead of golden branches. For it is not meet that she should be without arms, who is the spouse of Thracian Ares and a Lacedaemonian.

poems.title: Book XVI, 183: On a Statue of Dionysus which stood near Athena
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A. “Tell me what hast thou in common with Pallas; for to her javelins and wars, to thee banquets are exceeding dear.” B. “Do not rashly, O stranger, ask such questions about the gods, but learn in how many ways I am like to this goddess. For the glory of wars is dear to me likewise; all India, subdued by me as far as the Eastern Ocean, knows it. The race of mortals, too, have we gifted, she with the olive, and I with the sweet clusters of the vine. Neither again did a mother suffer the pangs of labour for me, but I burst from our father’s thigh, she from his head.”

poems.title: Book XVI, 185: On Statues of Dionysus and Heracles
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Both are from Thebes, both warriors, and both sons of Zeus. The one wields well his thyrsus, the other his club. The statues of both are close together and like are the arms they bear, the one a fawn-skin, the other a lion-skin; cymbals the one, a rattle the other. To both Hera was a cruel goddess, and both through fire went from earth to the immortals.

poems.title: Book XVI, 187: On another of the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A certain man prayed for help to a wooden Hermes, and Hermes remained wooden. Then, taking him up, the man threw him on the ground, and, the statue breaking, out from it poured gold. Outrage often produces profit.

poems.title: Book XVI, 192: On a Hermes by Scopas
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Stranger, deem not that thou lookest on one of the vulgar crowd of Hermae; for I am the work of Scopas.

poems.title: Book XVI, 194: On a Statue of Love made into a Frying-pan
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Someone has transferred this brazen Love from fire to fire, fitting a frying-pan on to him, torment to torment.

poems.title: Book XVI, 202: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Say not, stranger, that I am he from Lebanon, he who delights in the converse by night of youths who love the revel, I am a little Love and country-bred, the son of the Nymph who dwells hard by, and I further but the gardener’s labour. Hence from my dear fruitful plot I am crowned with four crowns by the four Seasons.

poems.title: Book XVI, 209: A Love Couplet
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou who dost blow on thy torch to light the lamp, come and light it from my soul. I am all aflame.

poems.title: Book XVI, 217: On a Statue of Calliope
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I am Calliope, and I gave to Cyrus my breast to suck, the breast which nourished divine Homer, and from whence sweet Orpheus drank.

poems.title: Book XVI, 223: On a Statue of Nemesis
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Nemesis warns us by her cubit-rule and bridle neither to do anything without measure nor to be unbridled in our speech.

poems.title: Book XVI, 224: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I, Nemesis, hold a cubit-rule. “Why?” you will say. I proclaim to all men, “Nothing beyond due measure.”

poems.title: Book XVI, 227: On a Statue of Hermes
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Throw thyself down here, wayfarer, on the green meadow, and rest thy languid limbs from painful toil; here where the pine also, tossed by the western breeze, shall soothe thee as thou listenest to the song of the cicadas, and the shepherd likewise on the hills, piping at mid-day by the fountain under the leafy plane-tree. Thus, having escaped the burning heat of the autumnal dog-star, thou shalt in good time cross the hill. Take this counsel that Hermes gives thee.

poems.title: Book XVI, 229: On a Picture of Pan
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This, our dearest one, is the issue of the loins of Zeus himself and the cloud over his head testifies to it. For Zeus the cloud-gatherer begot Hermes the King, and Hermes begot Pan the goatherd.

poems.title: Book XVI, 246: On Another
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Either a Satyr secretly entered the bronze, or the bronze, compelled by art, poured itself round a Satyr.

poems.title: Book XVI, 249
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: O thou who lookest on this lovely statue, seat thee near it and worship Aphrodite; and praise Glycera, the daughter of Dionysius, who set me up as an offering by the soft waves of the purple shore.

poems.title: Book XVI, 250: On Love
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: See how winged Love is breaking the winged thunderbolt, showing that there is a fire stronger than fire.

poems.title: Book XVI, 251: On Eros and Anteros
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Who fashioned a winged Love and set him opposite winged Love? Nemesis, taking vengeance on the bow with the bow, that he may suffer what he did; and he, the bold boy never daunted before, is crying as he tastes the bitter arrows, and thrice he spits in the deep folds of his bosom! Oh, most marvellous! One shall burn fire with fire, Love has touched Love to the quick.

poems.title: Book XVI, 252: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I, too, am of the blood of Cypris, and my mother exhorted me to take my bow and take wing against my brother.

poems.title: Book XVI, 253: On a Picture of unarmed Artemis
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A. Artemis, where are thy bow and the quiver that hung from thy neck? Where are thy Cretan hunting-boots and the buckle wrought of gold that gathers up thy purple robe as high as thy knee? B. That is the armour I don for the chase, but to my sacrifices I go as I am, to meet the holy incense cloud.

poems.title: Book XVI, 254: On a Statue of Hermes by the Roadside
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Men who pass by me have heaped up a pile of stones sacred to Hermes, and I, in return for their small kindness, give them no great thanks, but only say that it is seven stadia more to Goat Fountain.

poems.title: Book XVI, 255: On another Hermes guarding a Garden
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Wayfarer, come not near the vines, nor yet the apples, nor where the medlars grow, but pass me by there along the rope, so as not to disturb or break off any of these things which the gardener Midon got with labour. He it was who set me up here, but if thou give not ear to me, thou shalt know how Hermes rewards wicked men.

poems.title: Book XVI, 256: On another Hermes
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The place where I dwell is steep and desert, traveller; it is no fault of mine, but of Archelochus who set me up. For Hermes, Sir, is no lover of the mountains, no dweller on the hill-tops, but rather takes delight in roads; but Archelochus, being himself a lover of solitude and without neighbours, settled me, O passer by, beside him, making me even as he is.

poems.title: Book XVI, 257: On Dionysus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Lo from the fire for the second time, Dionysus, thou hast appeared in bronze. Myro gave thee a second birth.

poems.title: Book XVI, 258: On Pan
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: In the fane of Dictynna, where blaze the altar fires, did the Cretan erect me such as you see me in bronze, goat-footed Pan. I wear a skin and carry two hare-staves, and from the cave in the rock gaze with both eyes at the hill.

poems.title: Book XVI, 259: On the Statue of Pan on the Athenian Acropolis
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: On the citadel of Pallas did the Athenians set me up, trophy-bearing Pan wrought of Parian marble.

poems.title: Book XVI, 260: On a Statue of Priapus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: If I, Priapus, see you stepping near the kail, you thief, I will uncover your nakedness by the kail-bed itself. You will say that this is a shameful duty for a god to have. I know myself that it is shameful, but I would have you know that for this purpose I was set up.

poems.title: Book XVI, 262
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Goat-footed Pan with the wine-skin on his shoulder, and the Nymphs, and lovely Danae, are all by Praxiteles. They are all of marble, and the hands that wrought them were supremely skilled. Momus himself will cry out “Father Zeus, this was perfect skill.”

poems.title: Book XVI, 263: On the Nemesis of Phidias
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The Persians first brought me here, a stone to use for setting up the trophy of their victory, but now I am Nemesis. I stand here for both, a trophy of their victory for the Greeks, and for the Persians the Nemesis of war.

poems.title: Book XVI, 264: On a Procession to Isis
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: To Isis, parent of crops, mother of the corn, thousand-shaped, in a stone basket without the toiling plough, go of their own accord the fruits of the field, even to their mother.

poems.title: Book XVI, 264a
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: To the Nymphs is this statue dedicated, and the place is their care. Yea, may it be their care that a constant stream flow from the fountain.

poems.title: Book XVI, 265: On Momus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Who with blameless hands fashioned Blame the thrice accurst, who mourns at all good things? How the old man, like one alive throwing himself on the ground, seeks to find rest from his sorrows, his limbs heavy to him. They tell who he is, that deadly double row of teeth gnashing at the good fortune of the neighbours, that wasted burden of a body; on one of his senile hands he rests his bald head, and with the other, grinning sardonically, he plants his staff on the ground, quarrelling aimlessly with the lifeless rock.

poems.title: Book XVI, 266: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Waste away, starting from thy wretched nails, all-devouring Momus; waste and gnash thy poisoned jaws. They tell who thou art, those stretched sinews and the veins of thy limbs, and their dying strength devoid of flesh, and the harsh locks that hang over thy wrinkled forehead (one line missing). ‘Tell me, who fashioned thee so, the living plague of men, not leaving a place for thy teeth to fasten on?

poems.title: Book XVI, 268: In Praise of the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Either Apollo wrote thy words, Hippocrates, or thou art the witness of his healing power.

poems.title: Book XVI, 269: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is he who opened the secret paths of medicine, the divine healer of men, Hippocrates of Cos.

poems.title: Book XVI, 271: On Sosander, the Veterinary Surgeon
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou wast the healer of men, Hippocrates, but thou of horses too, Sosander, learned in the secrets of medicine. Either exchange your professions or your names. The one should not be named from the art of which the other was the master.

poems.title: Book XVI, 274: On Oribasius the Physician
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is the great physician of the Emperor Julian, divine Oribasius, right worthy of this pious gift; for he had a wise mind like a bee, gathering from this place and that the flowers of former physicians.

poems.title: Book XVI, 279: On the Lyre-playing Stone at Megara
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: As thou passest by Nisaea remember me, the musical stone; for when Alcathous was building his towered wall, then Phoebus lifted on his shoulder the building stone, laying down his Delphian lyre in me. Hence I am a lyrist; strike me with a small pebble and get evidence of what I boast.

poems.title: Book XVI, 280: On a Bath
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: With the money of Agathon did the people of Tegea build the bath here, a marvel to future generations too.

poems.title: Book XVI, 281: On a Bath at Praenetus in Bithynia
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: What is now a bath was formerly no bath, but a rubbish ground, a place of excretion; but now it excels in splendour those delightful and lovely baths of which all men sing the praises. For Alexander, the bishop of Nicaea, the star of illustrious learning, built it at his own expense.

poems.title: Book XVI, 289: On the Dancer Xenophon of Smyrna
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: We thought we were looking on Bacchus himself when the old man lustily led the Maenads in their furious dance, and played Cadmus tripping it in the fall of his years, and the messenger coming from the forest where he had spied on the rout of the Bacchants, and frenzied Agave exulting in the blood of her son. Heavens how divine was the man’s acting!

poems.title: Book XVI, 292: On the two Homeric Poems
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Homer, son of Meles, thou hast won eternal glory for Hellas and thy fatherland Colophon, and these two daughters didst thou beget by thy divine soul, writing from thy heart the twain tablets. The one sings the many wanderings of Odysseus in his home-coming, and the other the Trojan war.

poems.title: Book XVI, 293: On Homer
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Who wrote on his pages the Trojan war, and who the long wanderings of the son of Laertes? I cannot be certain about his name or his city. Heavenly Zeus, can it be that Homer gets the glory of thine own poems?

poems.title: Book XVI, 294: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Or what country shall we record Homer to be a citizen, the man to whom all cities reach out their hands? Is it not the truth that this is unknown, but the hero, like an immortal, left as a heritage to the Muses the secret of his country and race?

poems.title: Book XVI, 295: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: It was not the plain of Smyrna that gave birth to divine Homer; no, nor Colophon, the star of delicate Ionia; not Chios, nor fruitful Egypt, nor holy Cyprus, nor the rocky island that was the home of the son of Laertes, nor Argos, the land of Danaus, and Cyclops-built Mycenae, nor the city of the ancient sons of Cecrops. No, he was not Earth’s work, but the Muses sent him from the sky to bring desirable gifts to the creatures of a day.

poems.title: Book XVI, 297: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Seven cities claim to be the root of Homer: Cyme, Smyrna, Chios, Colophon, Pylos, Argos, Athens.

poems.title: Book XVI, 298: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Seven cities strive for the learned root of Homer: Smyrna, Chios, Colophon, Ithaca, Pylos, Argos, Athens.

poems.title: Book XVI, 299: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A. Wast thou a Chian? B. I say No. A. What then, a Smyrnian? B. I deny it. A. Was either Cyme or Colophon thy native place, Homer? B. Neither. A. Was Salamis thy city? B. No, I do not spring from her either. A. But tell me thyself where thou wast born. B. I will not. A. Wherefore? B. I know for sure that if I tell the truth, I shall make the other cities my enemies.

poems.title: Book XVI, 300: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou art besung, Homer, for all ages and from all ages for having won thee the glory of the heavenly Muse. For thou didst sing the wrath of Achilles and the confusion of the Greek ships whirled hither and thither on the sea, and Odysseus, the subtle-minded, worn out by his wanderings, the husband that Penelope rejoiced to see again.

poems.title: Book XVI, 301: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: If Homer be a god, let him be honoured as one of the gods; but if again he be not a god, let him be believed to be a god.

poems.title: Book XVI, 302: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Nature produced him; she produced him by a mighty effort, and after bearing him she ceased from her labour, having spent all her care on Homer alone.

poems.title: Book XVI, 303: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Who has not heard of the mighty voice of Homer? What land, what sea, does not know of the Grecian battle? The people of the Cimmerians, lacking the rays of the all-seeing Sun, has heard the name of Troy; Atlas has heard it, Atlas on whose shoulders broad-bosomed heaven rests.

poems.title: Book XVI, 304: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: By telling the burnt city’s story, Homer, thou hast allowed unsacked cities to envy her fate.

poems.title: Book XVI, 309: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou seest me, the old man of Teos never sated by loves, singing alike to young men and to maidens. But my eyes are heavy with wine, and I bear from my revelling the pleasant signs of sleepless night-festivals.

poems.title: Book XVI, 311: On Oppian’s Halieutics
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Oppian, collecting in his pages the tribes that swim the sea, served to all young men a dish of fish infinite in variety.

poems.title: Book XVI, 313: On a Statue of the Rhetor Ptolemy at Antioch
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A. Statue, who created thee? B. Eloquence. A. Whose art thou? B. Ptolemy’s. A. Which? B. The Cretan’s. A. Because of what? B. For merit. A. What kind of merit? B. All kinds. A. To whom? B. To lawyers. A. And does a wooden statue satisfy you? B. Yes, Ptolemy accepts no gold.

poems.title: Book XVI, 318: On the Portrait of a Dull Rhetor
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Who painted thee who speakest not in the character of a rhetor? Thou art silent, and dost not speak: nothing more lifelike.

poems.title: Book XVI, 319: On a Portrait of the Rhetor Marinus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Portraits are an honour dear to men, but for Marinus a portrait is an insult, as it exhibits the uncomeliness of his form.

poems.title: Book XVI, 320: On a Portrait of the Rhetor Aristides
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Aristides put an end to the ancient quarrel that the cities of Ionia had about Homer’s parentage. For they all say, “It was Smyrna who gave birth to divine Homer, even she who bore likewise the rhetor Aristides.”

poems.title: Book XVI, 326: On a Picture of the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The painter drew the very image of Pythagoras, and you would have seen him with his voice, too, had Pythagoras wished to speak.

poems.title: Book XVI, 329: On a Portrait of Aristotle
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is Aristotle measuring the earth and the starry heavens.

poems.title: Book XVI, 330: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Intellect and the soul of Aristotle, the picture of both is the same.

poems.title: Book XVI, 335: On Porphyrius
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The Emperor and the faction erected the statue of Porphyrius, son of Calchas, loaded with many crowns won by skilled toil, the youngest of all the drivers as well as the best, and winner of as many victories as any. This man’s statue should have been of gold, not of bronze like the others.

poems.title: Book XVI, 336: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Four times before did the people shout distinctly, desiring Porphyrius, the son of Calchas; but he, taking up the reins and his driving belt at the right of the Emperor’s seat drives, starting from there, urging on his team, and in the middle of his racing career his bronze statue was erected with the first down on his cheeks. If this honour came to him quicker than years, yet it came late after victories won by much labour, after many crowns.

poems.title: Book XVI, 337: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Cytherea was in love with Anchises and Selene with Endymion, and now it seems that Victory is in love with Porphyrius, who, ever changing his own team for that of another driver of his faction, was often crowned in the races that lasted all day without labour on his part, his companion only following him.

poems.title: Book XVI, 338: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Victory gave to thee, Porphyrius, while still young, this honour which time has given to others late in life and grudgingly; for, having counted the performances that won thee many crowns, she found them superior to those of old drivers. Why did not the rival faction, in admiration of thy glory, applaud thee loudly? Blessed is the most free people of the Blues, to whom our great Emperor granted thee as a gift.

poems.title: Book XVI, 339: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The valiant to the valiant; the wise to the wise; the sons of victory, the Blues, to the son of victory, Porphyrius, erected this statue; for he glories in the two victories he gained by the interchanged teams, the team he gave and the team he received.

poems.title: Book XVI, 340: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: To others when they have retired, but to Porphyrius alone while still racing, did the Emperor give this honour. For often he drove his own horses to victory and then took in hand the team of his adversary, and was again crowned. Hence arose a keen rivalry on the part of the Greens, hence a shout of applause for him, O King, who will give joy both to Blues and to Greens.

poems.title: Book XVI, 341: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The votes of all erected near to Victory the statue of me, Porphyrius, while still driving. For my own faction demanded the honour, and the opposite one desired to have me again, renouncing their hostility. I got the best of the other drivers by my cleverness, giving them in exchange for their own better horses, and then showing them to be my inferiors.

poems.title: Book XVI, 342: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The sculptor exactly portrayed in bronze Porphyrius himself, fashioning him as if alive. But who shall mould his grace, his races, the inspired tricks of his craft, and victory that never varied?

poems.title: Book XVI, 343: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: In a brazen image the Lord of the Latins set up the victorious driver, strong himself as brass, as being skilled and dear to the Blues; but we shall see many statues yet of Porphyrius erected because of his victories.

poems.title: Book XVI, 344: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A. Who art thou, dear young man, the point of thy chin just marked with down? B. Stranger, I am Porphyrius. A. Thy country? B. Africa. A. Who hath honoured thee? B. The Emperor, on account of my driving. A. Who testifies to it? B. The faction of the Blues. A. Porphyrius, thou shouldst have had Lysippus, a skilled sculptor, to testify to so many victories.

poems.title: Book XVI, 345: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou standest near Victory and King Alexander, thou who hast gathered thee the glory of both.

poems.title: Book XVI, 346: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This eye of Fortune ranges over all things, but now the eye of Fortune is attracted to the exploits of Porphyrius alone.

poems.title: Book XVI, 347: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The people, in admiration of thy whirling whip and thy shield, was minded to set thee up in two aspects as was fitting, as a strong driver and a strong warrior; but the bronze, forming itself like thy soul, would not flow in two streams.

poems.title: Book XVI, 348: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Why did the distinguished faction of the Greens erect on the course the statue of the charioteer Porphyrius? The Emperor himself issued the order. What could he do, but honour him in view of his good will to him and of his skill as a driver?

poems.title: Book XVI, 349: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Our Sovereign Lord, who grants this favour to the Greens, gave to Porphyrius after the races an honour worthy of his performances. For often the people, their attention turned to exploits more than usually brilliant, praised Calliopas and again Porphyrius, the two names that belonged to this brazen hero, who won the meed of valour in the chariot-races.

poems.title: Book XVI, 350: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Not only did divine Victory crown thee on the race-course, but in war, too, she showed thee to be victorious, then when the Emperor, with the Greens to assist him, warred with the furiously raging enemy of the throne; when the savage tyrant fell, as Rome was on the point of perishing, and the light of Latin liberty came back. Therefore the Monarch gave to the Greens the privileges they formerly had, and the artist wrought and polished thy image, Porphyrius.

poems.title: Book XVI, 351: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: THe crowns from the hostile faction too, Porphyrius, are unimpeachable witnesses of thy exploits. For ever in the race thou conquerest one after the other all the rival charioteers, a mere toy for thy skilled hands. Therefore hast thou alone gained an unwonted mark of honour, a bronze statue in the grounds of each faction.

poems.title: Book XVI, 352: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The sculptor made the bronze like unto the charioteer, but would that he could have fashioned also the vastness of his skill, its vastness and beauty, a thing that when Nature brought forth late in her life she swore, “I cannot travail again.” She swore it with truthful lips, for to Porphyrius first and alone she gave all her gifts.

poems.title: Book XVI, 353: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: If envy could be at rest and chose to judge the contests, all men testify to the achievements of Porphyrius. Yea, perchance they would say after reckoning up his races, “That is a slender reward for so much exertion.” For, having gathered into one all the separate qualities which adorn each driver, he showed himself to be the great man he is.

poems.title: Book XVI, 354: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thrice-desired Porphyrius, the city reverencing thee honours thee with a bronze statue. She would have wished it to be gold, but Nemesis was before her eyes. But if thy well-wishers, the faction of the Greens, never cease celebrating thy wonted victories, they are every man of them living statues in thy honour, and all gold is worthless in comparison with them.

poems.title: Book XVI, 355: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Nor yet has Fortune worthily rewarded thy hard-won victories, for thy victories are greater than the prizes that have fallen to thee. But remain now in this, the first of the factions, the more constant and more excellent, consuming the envious hearts of our enemies, who, seeing thy whip ever victorious, never cease to blame their own recklessness.

poems.title: Book XVI, 356: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Time is the cause of the honours of others, and those who are judged worthy of them, owing to their victories, do not lack grey hairs, but lack that virtue on which glory depends. Porphyrius alone twice gained the splendour of such gifts, not boasting many decades of years, but many hundreds of victories, and all of them akin to the Graces.

poems.title: Book XVI, 358: On the Same under his other name, Calliopas
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: When a youth thou didst conquer thy elders, and now, in thy later years, thou conquerest the young drivers of racing four-horse chariots. Having accomplished thy six decades of years, thou hast won, Calliopas, a statue for thy victories, by command of the Emperor, so that thy renown may abide for future ages. Would that thy body were as immortal as thy renown.

poems.title: Book XVI, 359: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Victory, the charioteer, dedicated to thee, Calliopas, this brazen image of thy divine form, because in thy old age thou didst conquer men in the prime of youth by thy force in subduing horses, and in thy youth didst conquer thy elders by skill. Hence the faction of the Blues, the children of liberty, erected two prizes for thee, one for thy art and the other for thy force.

poems.title: Book XVI, 360: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thy old age has surpassed thy youth in victories, and thou didst ever overcome all, Calliopas. Therefore do the Emperor and this free faction again raise this honour for thee, a monument of thy skill and valour.

poems.title: Book XVI, 361: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: O Calliopas, thou who raisest applause in the theatre, this is thy portrait which a swarm of much-envied crowns raises to thee. For neither did any charioteer cozen thee, nor did any hard-mouthed horse’s jaws refuse to obey thy reins. Alone hast thou gained the reward of victory; verily the opinion of all is that by contending thou leavest prizes for others.

poems.title: Book XVI, 362: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: O Calliopas, celebrated for thy achievements, what does it profit thee that thy labours are rewarded with a bronze statue by the Emperor, by this myriadthroated faction, by the whole city, considering that even the hands of the hostile faction applauded thy exploits?

poems.title: Book XVI, 363: On Faustinus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Wits are the mothers of a winner’s honours, not the force of youth, nor swift driving, nor favourable occasion. May thy mind, Faustinus, be propitious, which takes precedence of all these things, and whose companion is immortal Victory.

poems.title: Book XVI, 364: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Formerly in thy youth, Faustinus, the minds of the old men feared thee, and now the strength of the young men trembles before thine in thy advanced years. The first place was ever gained for thee by thy toil, which brings honour to thee, an old man among the youths, a youth among the old men.

poems.title: Book XVI, 365: On Constantinus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Since Constantinus entered the house of Hades the race-course is full of despondency, and pleasure has abandoned the spectators, nor even in the streets does one see the old friendly strife.

poems.title: Book XVI, 366: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The citizens, mourning thee, erected thy image, Constantinus, to be a delight to thy departed spirit. When the people confirmed thy fame on thy death, the Emperor, too, was mindful of thy exertions after thy decease, because the abusive art of driving has perished, ceasing finally with thee as it began with thee.

poems.title: Book XVI, 367: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: While Constantinus yet lived, the city deemed a bronze statue a small reward for him, for the whole people knew how many crowns in his long racing career he had set on his head because of glorious Victory. But when he died, in regret for him, it erected this his dear form, so that posterity, too, should be kept mindful of his achievements.

poems.title: Book XVI, 368: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The Blues and Greens, always at variance, shouted aloud one concordant decision, that thou, Constantinus, shouldst have on thy tomb this ornament, acclaimed by all, pleasing to all.

poems.title: Book XVI, 369: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Immortal Constantinus, thy course, high in the light, has traversed the boundaries of east, west, south, and north. Let none say thou art dead, for even Hades cannot lay his hand on the invincible.

poems.title: Book XVI, 370: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This, his statue, has been placed near those of his own family, for it was proper that they should stand in one place, the three who won equal glory for their skill in the race, gaining equal swarms of innumerable crowns.

poems.title: Book XVI, 371: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Here the city erected Constantinus, son of Faustinus, next his own family, the best of all charioteers. For through all the long time he raced he never failed, but ended by a victory, as he had formerly begun by a victory. When he was a young man the older drivers who had won crowns on the course appointed him president of the races.

poems.title: Book XVI, 372: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is a gift for thee, Constantinus, from thy nurse, Victory, who hath followed thee from thy childhood all through thy life. For in the five times ten years thou didst pass on the race-course thou didst never light on thy equal, or even on one a little inferior to thee; but while yet a lad and beardless thou didst conquer men, when grown up thou didst conquer those of thine age, and in thine old age the young men.

poems.title: Book XVI, 373: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The city wished Constantinus to wield the reins for ever; she wished it, but Nature refused to grant her desire. Therefore she bethought her of erecting this statue to console her for her lost love, that time and oblivion should not envelop him, but that he might remain, the desire of his lovers, the envy of charioteers, an ornament to the course, and a tale for future generations to tell; and that one in time to come, looking on inferior drivers, should bless the former age that looked on him.

poems.title: Book XVI, 374: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Constantinus having won five-and-twenty races on one morning, changed his team with his rival’s, and taking the same horses that he had formerly beaten, won twenty-one times with them. Often there was a great strife between the two factions as to which was to have him, and they gave him two robes to choose from.

poems.title: Book XVI, 375: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Awake, Constantinus! Why dost thou sleep the brazen sleep? The people long to see thy team on the course, and the charioteers, lacking thy instruction, sit just like orphaned children.

poems.title: Book XVI, 376: On Uranius
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Uranius, who had distinguished himself in the service of both the factions, gained glory from both while still driving. His first reward came from the Greens, and stands near their stand. They also, when he had retired from racing, brought him back again to the chariots, mindful of his former victory.

poems.title: Book XVI, 377: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The Emperor, when Uranius had retired from the race-course after gaining splendid victories, made him mount again his victorious chariot, doing a favour to all the factions; for the city has no desire for the races without Uranius. Therefore, admiring him for his first victories and his last, the city erected his statue during the second period of his career.

poems.title: Book XVI, 378: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Uranius has Nicaea and New Rome near him, being a native of one and having gained glory in the other. He wins from both sides, because he was very clever at dashing forward and getting past on both sides of the course. Therefore did they portray him in golden metal, the precious charioteer in the most precious of possessions.

poems.title: Book XVI, 380: On Porphyrius, of the faction of the Blues
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Porphyrius, the wonder of the Blues, having conquered every charioteer on earth, does well to rise and race towards heaven. For he, victorious over every driver here below, mounts to join the sun on its course.

poems.title: Book XVI, 381: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This Porphyrius, son of Calchas, with the first down on his cheeks, held the reins for the faction of the Blues. I marvel how some artist’s hand has painted his horses as if alive. Really, if he whips them again, I think he will be carried again to victory.

poems.title: Book XVI, 382: On Faustinus, of the faction of the Greens
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Look on the work of the architect of this house. For if it had not been covered by a strong roof Faustinus, the ancient glory of the Greens, would have mounted racing to heaven, so like the life are he and his team. Take the roof off and he will reach the sky.

poems.title: Book XVI, 383: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is Faustinus, the former charioteer, after engaging whom the faction of the Greens never knew what defeat was in the race. He was old, as you see, but in his strength he was as a young man, and was never once vanquished.

poems.title: Book XVI, 384: On Constantinus the Charioteer of the Whites
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Constantinus, wielding the reins of the White faction, were he not restrained by the solidity of the house, would conquer those three, getting to heaven first. You would see him mount the heavens without breath. The artist persuades me that I see him alive.

poems.title: Book XVI, 385: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Constantinus was his name, but in the old days he skilfully drove the four-horse chariot of the Whites. Since Charon carried him off, it is set, the light of horse-racing and all the delight and art of the theatre.

poems.title: Book XVI, 386: On Julianus the Charioteer of the Reds
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The hand of man knows how to give birth to men long ago dead, for Julianus is as strong here as of old, guiding this way and that the reins of the Red faction. Now he stands painted here on high, himself and his chariot; his hand awaits the signal. Give him a winning-post.

poems.title: Book XVI, 387: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This Julianus, with his car of the Red faction, conquered his adversaries in the race. But if the painter had endued him with breath he is ready again to drive his chariot and come in first, and even take the Crown.

poems.title: Rose (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Would I were a pink rose, that fastening me with thine hands thou mightest grant me grace of thy snowy breast.

poems.title: Love's Excess (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Arm thyself, Cypris, with thy bow, and go at thy leisure to some other mark; for I have not even room left for a wound.

poems.title: To Pan Paean (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: This for thee, O pipe-player, minstrel, gracious god, holy lord of the Naiads who pour their urns, Hyginus made as a gift, whom thou, O king, didst draw nigh and make whole of his hard sickness; for among all my children thou didst stand by me visibly, not in a dream of night, but about the mid-circle of the day.

poems.title: To Aphrodite, with a Talisman (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Nico's wryneck, that knows how to draw a man even from overseas, and girls out of their wedding-chambers, chased with gold, carven out of translucent amethyst, lies before thee, Cyprian, for thine own possession, tied across the middle with a soft lock of purple lamb's wool, the gift of the sorceress of Larissa.

poems.title: To the Orchard God (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: This fresh-cloven pomegranate and fresh-downed quince, and the wrinkled navel-like fig, and the purple grape-bunch spirting wine, thick-clustered, and the nut fresh-stripped of its green husk, to this rustic staked Priapus the keeper of the fruit dedicates, an offering from his orchard trees.

poems.title: To the Gods of the Farm (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: To Pan of the goats and fruitful Dionysus and Demeter Lady of Earth I dedicate a common offering, and beseech of them fair fleeces and fair wine and fair fruit of the corn-ears in my reaping.

poems.title: To Pan of the Fountain (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: We supplicate Pan, the goer on the cliffs, twy-horned leader of the Nymphs, who abides in this house of rock, to be gracious to us, whosoever come to this spring of ever-flowing drink to rid us of our thirst.

poems.title: To Pan of the Shepherds (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: O Pan, utter thy holy voice to the feeding flocks, running thy curved lip over the golden reeds, that so they may often bring gifts of white milk in heavy udders to Clymenus' home, and for thee the lord of the she-goats, standing fairly by thy altars, may spirt the red blood from his shaggy breast.

poems.title: On the Dead in a Battle in Boeotia (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: O Time, all-surveying deity of the manifold things wrought among mortals, carry to all men the message of our fate, that striving to save the holy soil of Greece we die on the renowned Boeotian plains.

poems.title: On the Grave of an Athenian at Meroë (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Straight is the descent to Hades, whether thou wert to go from Athens or takest thy journey from Meroë; let it not vex thee to have died so far away from home; from all lands the wind that blows to Hades is but one.

poems.title: On the Same (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Mariner, ask not whose tomb I am here, but be thine own fortune a kinder sea.

poems.title: On the Children of Nicander and Lysidice (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: This is the single tomb of Nicander's children; the light of a single morning ended the sacred offspring of Lysidice.

poems.title: On a Baby (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Me a baby that was just tasting life heaven snatched away, I know not whether for good or for evil; insatiable Death, why hast thou snatched me cruelly in infancy? why hurriest thou? Are we not all thine in the end?

poems.title: On a Child of Seven (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Hermes messenger of Persephone, whom usherest thou thus to the laughterless abyss of Death? what hard fate snatched Ariston from the fresh air at seven years old? and the child stands between his parents. Pluto delighting in tears, are not all mortal spirits allotted to thee? why gatherest thou the unripe grapes of youth?

poems.title: On Cleoetes (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Looking on the monument of a dead boy, Cleoetes son of Menesaechmus, pity him who was beautiful and died.

poems.title: On a Beautiful Boy (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Not death is bitter, since that is the fate of all, but to die ere the time and before our parents: I having seen not marriage nor wedding-chant nor bridal bed, lie here the love of many, and to be the love of more.

poems.title: On a Boy of Nineteen (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Bidding hail to me, Diogenes beneath the earth, go about thy business and obtain thy desire; for at nineteen years old I was laid low by cruel sickness and leave the sweet sun.

poems.title: On a Singing-Girl (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Blue-eyed Musa, the sweet-voiced nightingale, suddenly this little grave holds voiceless, and she lies like a stone who was so accomplished and so famous; fair Musa, be this dust light over thee.

poems.title: On Claudia Homonoea (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I Homonoea, who was far clearer-voiced than the Sirens, I who was more golden than the Cyprian herself at revellings and feasts, I the chattering bright swallow lie here, leaving tears to Atimetus, to whom I was dear from girlhood; but unforeseen fate scattered all that great affection.

poems.title: On a Mother of Eighteen, and Her Baby (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Name me Polyxena wife of Archelaus, child of Theodectes and hapless Demarete, and a mother as far as the birth-pangs; but fate overtook the child before full twenty suns, and myself died at eighteen years, just a mother and just a bride, so brief was all my day.

poems.title: On a Young Wife (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: To his wife Paulina, holy of life and blameless, who died at nineteen years, Andronicus the physician paying memorial placed this witness the last of all.

poems.title: On Atthis of Cnidos (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Atthis who didst live for me and breathe thy last toward me, source of joyfulness formerly as now of tears, holy, much lamented, how sleepest thou the mournful sleep, thou whose head was never laid away from thy husband's breast, leaving Theius alone as one who is no more; for with thee the hopes of our life went to darkness.

poems.title: On Amazonia of Thessalonica (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Why idly bemoaning linger you by my tomb? nothing worthy of lamentation is mine among the dead. Cease from plaints and be at rest, O husband, and you my children fare well, and keep the memory of Amazonia.

poems.title: On a Lacedaemonian Nurse (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Here earth holds the Peloponnesian woman who was the most faithful nurse of the children of Diogeitus.

poems.title: On a Persian Slave (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Even now beneath the earth I abide faithful to thee, yes my master, as before, forgetting not thy kindness, in that then thou broughtest me thrice out of sickness to safe foothold, and now didst lay me here beneath sufficient shelter, calling me by name, Manes the Persian; and for thy good deeds to me thou shalt have servants readier at need.

poems.title: On a Favourite Dog (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Thou who passest on the path, if haply thou dost mark this monument, laugh not, I pray thee, though it is a dog's grave; tears fell for me, and the dust was heaped above me by a master's hands, who likewise engraved these words on my tomb.

poems.title: On a Dead Friend (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: This little stone, good Sabinus, is the record of our great friendship; ever will I require thee; and thou, if it is permitted, drink not among the dead of the water of Lethe for me.

poems.title: On an Unhappy Man (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I Dionysius of Tarsus lie here at sixty, having never married; and would that my father had not.

poems.title: The Grove of the Muses (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Say thou that this grave is consecrate to the Muses, pointing to the books by the plane-trees, and that we guard it; and if a true lover of ours come hither, we crown him with our ivy.

poems.title: Erinna (1) (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Thee, as thou wert just giving birth to a springtide of honeyed songs and just finding thy swan-voice, Fate, mistress of the threaded spindle, drove to Acheron across the wide water of the dead; but the fair labour of thy verses, Erinna, cries that thou art not perished, but keepest mingled choir with the Maidens of Pieria.

poems.title: Anacreon's Grave (1) (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: O stranger who passest this the tomb of Anacreon, pour libation over me in going by; for I am a drinker of wine.

poems.title: Calamus (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I the reed was a useless plant; for out of me grew not figs nor apple nor grape-cluster; but man consecrated me a daughter of Helicon, piercing my delicate lips and making me the channel of a narrow stream; and thenceforth, whenever I sip black drink, like one inspired I speak all words with this voiceless mouth.

poems.title: The Phaedo of Plato (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: If Plato did not write me, there were two Platos; I carry in me all the flowers of Socratic talk. But Panaetius concluded me to be spurious; yes, he who concluded that the soul was mortal, would conclude me spurious as well.

poems.title: On a Relief of Eros and Anteros (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Nemesis fashioned a winged Love contrary to winged Love, warding off bow with bow, that he may be done by as he did; and, bold and fearless before, he sheds tears, having tasted of the bitter arrows, and spits thrice into his low-girt bosom. Ah, most wonderful! one will burn with fire: Love has set Love aflame.

poems.title: On a Love Breaking the Thunderbolt (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Lo, how winged Love breaks the winged thunderbolt, showing that he is a fire more potent than fire.

poems.title: On a Statue of the Armed Venus (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Pallas said, seeing Cytherea armed, "O Cyprian, wilt thou that we go so to judgment?" and she, laughing softly, "why should I lift a shield in contest? if I conquer when naked, how will it be when I take arms?"

poems.title: On the Cnidian Venus of Praxiteles (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: The Cyprian said when she saw the Cyprian of Cnidus, "Alas where did Praxiteles see me naked?"

poems.title: On a Sleeping Ariadne (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Strangers, touch not the marble Ariadne, lest she even start up on the quest of Theseus.

poems.title: On a Niobe by Praxiteles (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: From life the gods made me a stone; and from stone again Praxiteles wrought me into life.

poems.title: On the Heifer of Myron (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Ah thou wert not quick enough, Myron, in thy casting; but the bronze grew solid before thou hadst cast in a soul.

poems.title: Zeus of the Fair Wind (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Let one call from the stern on Zeus the Fair Wind for guide on his road, shaking out sail against the forestays; whether he runs to the Dark Eddies, where Poseidon rolls his curling wave along the sands, or whether he searches the backward passage down the Aegean sea-plain, let him lay honey-cakes by this image, and so go his way; here Philon, son of Antipater, set up the ever-gracious god for pledge of fair and fortunate voyaging.

poems.title: Hermes of the Ways (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Go and rest your limbs here for a little under the juniper, O wayfarers, by Hermes, Guardian of the Way, not in crowds, but those of you whose knees are tired with heavy toil and thirst after traversing a long road; for there a breeze and a shady seat and the fountain under the rock will lull your toil-wearied limbs; and having so escaped the midday breath of the autumnal dogstar, as is right, honour Hermes of the Ways.

poems.title: The Service of God (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Me Chelidon, priestess of Zeus, who knew well in old age how to make offering on the altars of the immortals, happy in my children, free from grief, the tomb holds; for with no shadow in their eyes the gods saw my piety.

poems.title: Beati Mundo Corde (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: He who enters the incense-filled temple must be holy; and holiness is to have a pure mind.

poems.title: The Water of Purity (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Hallowed in soul, O stranger, come even into the precinct of a pure god, touching thyself with the virgin water; for the good a few drops are set; but a wicked man the whole ocean cannot wash in its waters.

poems.title: The Garden God (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Call me not him who comes from Libanus, O stranger, who delights in the talk of young men love-making by night; I am small and a rustic, born of a neighbour nymph, and all my business is labour of the garden; whence four garlands at the hands of the four Seasons crown me from the beloved fruitful threshing-floor.

poems.title: The Meadow at Noon (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Here fling thyself down on the grassy meadow, O traveller, and rest thy relaxed limbs from painful weariness; since here also, as thou listenest to the cicalas' tune, the stone-pine trembling in the wafts of west wind will lull thee, and the shepherd on the mountains piping at noon nigh the spring under a copse of leafy plane: so escaping the ardours of the autumnal dogstar thou wilt cross the height to-morrow; trust this good counsel that Pan gives thee.

poems.title: Wood-Music (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Come and sit under my stone-pine that murmurs so honey-sweet as it bends to the soft western breeze; and lo this honey-dropping fountain, where I bring sweet sleep playing on my lonely reeds.

poems.title: The Singing Stone (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Remember me the singing stone, thou who passest by Nisaea; for when Alcathous was building his bastions, then Phoebus lifted on his shoulder a stone for the house, and laid down on me his Delphic harp; thenceforth I am lyre-voiced; strike me lightly with a little pebble, and carry away witness of my boast.

poems.title: The Woodland Well (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I the ever-flowing Clear Fount gush forth for by-passing wayfarers from the neighbouring dell; and everywhere I am bordered well with planes and soft-bloomed laurels, and make coolness and shade to lie in. Therefore pass me not by in summer; rest by me in quiet, ridding thee of thirst and weariness.

poems.title: The Complaint of the Cicala (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Why in merciless chase, shepherds, do you tear me the solitude-haunting cricket from the dewy sprays, me the roadside nightingale of the Nymphs, who at midday talk shrilly in the hills and the shady dells? Lo, here is the thrust and the blackbird, lo here such flocks of starlings, plunderers of the cornfield's riches; it is allowed to seize the ravagers of your fruits: destroy them: why grudge me my leaves and fresh dew?

poems.title: The Lighthouse (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: No longer dreading the rayless night-mist, sail towards me confidently, O seafarers; for all wanderers I light my far-shining torch, memorial of the labours of the Asclepiadae.

poems.title: Goodbye to Childhood (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Her tambourines and pretty ball, and the net that confined her hair, and her dolls and dolls' dresses, Timareta dedicates before her marriage to Artemis of Limnae, a maiden to a maiden, as is fit; do thou, daughter of Leto, laying thine hand over the girl Timareta, preserve her purely in her purity.

poems.title: The Unbroken Home (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Androtion built me, a burying-place for himself and his children and wife, but as yet I am the tomb of no one; so likewise may I remain for a long time; and if it must be, let me take to myself the eldest first.

poems.title: Left Alone (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Marathonis laid Nicopolis in this stone, wetting the marble coffin with tears, but all to no avail; for what is there more than sorrow for a man alone upon earth when his wife is gone?

poems.title: Rose and Thorn (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: The rose is at her prime a little while; which once past, thou wilt find when thou seekest no rose, but a thorn.

poems.title: Fortune's Plaything (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Not of good-will has Fortune advanced thee; but that she may show her omnipotence, even down to thee.

poems.title: Sparta (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: O Lacedaemon, once unsubdued and untrodden, thou seest shadeless the smoke of Olenian camp-fires on the Eurotas, and the birds building their nests on the ground wail for thee, and the wolves to do not hear any sheep.

poems.title: Berytus (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Formerly the dead left their city living; but we living hold the city's funeral.

poems.title: Youth and Riches (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I was young, but poor; now in old age I am rich, alas, alone of all men pitiable in both, who then could enjoy when I had nothing, and now have when I cannot enjoy.

poems.title: Tenants at Will (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I was once the field of Achaemenides, now I am Menippus', and again I shall pass from another to another; for the former thought once that he owned me, and the latter thinks so now in his turn; and I belong to no man at all, but to Fortune.

poems.title: Parting Company (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Hope, and thou Fortune, a long farewell; I have found the haven; there is nothing more between me and you; make your sport of those who come after me.

poems.title: A Jug of Wine (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Round-bellied, deftly-turned, one eared, long-throated, straight-necked, bubbling in thy narrow mouth, blithe handmaiden of Bacchus and the Muses and Cytherea, sweet of laughter, delightful ministress of social banquets, why when I am sober art thou in liquor, and when I am drunk, art sober again? Thou wrongest the good-fellowship of drinking.

poems.title: Dum Vivimus Vivamus (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Six hours fit labour best: and those that follow, shown forth in letters, say to mortals, "Live."

poems.title: Hope and Experience (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Whoso has married once and again seeks a second wedding, is a shipwrecked man who sails twice through a difficult gulf.

poems.title: A School of Rhetoric (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: All hail, seven pupils of Aristides the rhetorician, four walls and three benches.

poems.title: A Generation of Vipers (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Keep clear of a cobra, a toad, a viper, and the Laodiceans; also of a mad dog, and of the Laodiceans once again.

poems.title: Vegetarianism (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: You were not alone in keeping your hands off live things; we do so too; who touches live food, Pythagoras? but we eat what has been boiled and roasted and pickled, and there is no life in it then.

poems.title: Dusty Death (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Pay no offering of ointments or garlands on my stony tomb, nor make the fire blaze up; the expense is in vain. While I live be kind to me if thou wilt; but drenching my ashes with wine thou wilt make mire, and the dead man will not drink.

poems.title: Bene Merenti (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Dear Earth, take old Amyntichus to thy bosom, remembering his many labours on thee; for ever he planted in thee the olive-stock, and often made thee fair with vine-cuttings, and filled thee full of corn, and, drawing channels of water along, made thee rich with herbs and plenteous in fruit: do thou in return lie softly over his grey temples and flower into tresses of spring herbage.

poems.title: Loca Pastorum Deserta (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Naiads and chill cattle-pastures, tell to the bees when they come on their springtide way, that old Leucippus perished on a winter's night, setting snares for scampering hares, and no longer is the tending of the hives dear to him; but the pastoral dells mourn sore for him who dwelt with the mountain peak for neighbour.

poems.title: A Winter Voyage (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Thee too, son of Cleanor, desire after thy native land destroyed, trusting to the wintry gust of the South; for the unsecured season entangled thee, and the wet waves washed away thy lovely youth.

poems.title: The Dead Child (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Not yet were thy tresses cut, nor had the monthly courses of the moon driven a three years' space, O poor Cleodicus, when thy mother Nicasis, clasping thy coffin, wailed long over thy lamented grave, and thy father Pericleitus; but an unknown Acheron thou shalt flower out the youth that never, never returns.

poems.title: Persephone's Plaything (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Hades inexorable and inflexible, why hast thou thus reft infant Callaeschrus of life? Surely the child will be a plaything in the palace of Persephone, but at home he has left bitter sorrows.

poems.title: First Friendship (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Ah blessed one, dearest companion of the immortal Muses, fare thou well even in the house of Hades, Callimachus.

poems.title: Strewings for Graves (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: May flowers grow thick on thy newly-built tomb, not the dry bramble, not the evil weed, but violets and margerain and wet narcissus, Vibius, and around thee may all be roses.

poems.title: Mors Immortalis (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I died, but I await thee; and thou too shalt await some one else: one Death receives all mortals alike.

poems.title: Donec Hodie (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Drink and be merry; for what is to-morrow or what the future? no man knows. Run not, labour not; as thou canst, give, share, consume, be mortal-minded; to be alive and not to be alive are no way at all apart. All life is such, only the turn of the scale; if thou art beforehand, it is thine; and if thou diest, all is another's, and thou hast nothing.

poems.title: The Coffin-Maker (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I would have liked to be rich as Croesus of old was rich, and to be king of great Asia; but when I look on Nicanor the coffin-maker, and know for what he is making these flute-cases of his, sprinkling my flour and wetting it with my jug of wine, I sell all Asia for ointments and garlands.

poems.title: A Life's Wandering (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Know ye the flowery fields of the Cappadocian nation? thence I was born of good parents: since I left them I have wandered to the sunset and the dawn; my name was Glaphyrus, and like my mind. I lived out my sixtieth year in perfect freedom; I know both the favour of Fortune and the bitterness of life.

poems.title: The Shadow of Death (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Those who have left the sweet light I bewail no longer, but those who live ever in expectation of death.

poems.title: The Limit of Vision (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Now we flourish as before others did, and soon others will, whose children we shall never see.

poems.title: The Sum of Knowledge (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I was not, I came to be; I was, I am not: that is all; and who shall say more, will lie: I shall not be.

poems.title: Nepenthe (Mackail)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: How was I born? whence am I? why did I come? to go again: how can I learn anything, knowing nothing? Being nothing, I was born; again I shall be as I was before; nothing and nothing-worth is the human race. But come, serve to me the joyous fountain of Bacchus; for this is the drug counter-charming ills.

poems.title: Anacreon's Grave
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text:
You that pass this place of graves
  Pause and spill a cup for me,
For I hold Anacreon's ashes,
  And would drink as once would he.

poems.title: Friendship's Epitaph
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text:
This stone, my good Sabinus, although it be but small,
Shall be of our great friendship a witness unto all.
Ever shall I desire thee, and thou, if this may be,
Forbear to drink among the dead the lethe-draft for me.

poems.title: The Counsel of Pan
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text:
In this green meadow, traveller, yield
  Thy weary limbs to rest:
The branches of the stone pine sway
  To the wind from out the west;
The cricket calls, and all noon long
  The shepherd's piping fills
The plane-grove's leafy shadows
  By the spring among the hills.
Soothed by these sounds thou shalt avoid
  The dogstar's autumn fires,
And then to-morrow cross the ridge;--
  Such wisdom Pan inspires.

poems.title: Bénitier
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text:
Touch but the virgin water, clean of soul,
  Nor fear to pass into the pure god's sight:
For the good a drop suffices. But the whole
  Great ocean could not wash the unclean white.

poems.title: The End of the Comedy
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text:
Fortune and Hope, a long adieu!
  My ship is safe in port.
With me is nothing left to do,
  Make other lives your sport.
